utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody. Madam Registrar. Please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-06-90-T, the Prosecutor versus Gotovina, Cermak, and Markac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. The Defence of Mr. Gotovina has announced that it would like to make an opening statement. The other parties have announced they would not, at least not at this stage, therefore, Mr. Misetic or Mr. Kehoe, are you ready to give your opening statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, learned colleagues on the Defence and the Prosecution. Mr. President, Your Honours, my name is Gregory Kehoe. I am honoured here to represent the man General Ante Gotovina in this matter before the Court. I sat here yesterday for the better part of the day, Your Honours, and thought about many of the things that were being stated about General Gotovina by the Prosecution. I don't know where this has gone wrong. I don't know how the Office of the Prosecutor has gotten this so wrong, but we will attempt at this part of the opening to begin to explain and to elaborate, and my portion of the opening, Mr. President and Your Honours, I will talk about the general overview of the area. I will then turn to my colleague, Mr. Misetic, who will then talk about Operation Storm and the participation of General Gotovina in detail. As I sat here yesterday and listened to what was said by the Prosecution, it was not so much what the Prosecution said but what they didn't say that was starkly evident. What was starkly evident was that there was no deportation once Operation Storm commenced on the morning of August the 4th of 1995, because the Republic of Serb Krajina had always planned to remove their people from the area, a matter that was never brought forth to the Court. There was no excessive shelling of Knin on either the 4th or the 5th. How do we know that? We know that from very practical concerns, practical concerns that were evident to the Prosecution that they chose not to share. And the first and foremost practical concern being brought forth to the Court is the Brioni tape to both Mr. Tieger and Mr. Waespi referred, and in that tape President Tudjman cautions General Gotovina and the other military commanders not to expend unnecessary rounds. "Do not shell like we are Americans and Russians because we do not have the munitions." A fact that wasn't brought out by the Prosecution, yet starkly evident in the face of their argument that there was excessive shelling. They didn't bring out that the one person that the United Nations had tasked in Knin to determine whether civilian targets had been shelled, Steinar Hjertnes, who is the chief of the UN military observers, did such an examination on the 18th of August, and in that examination he concluded that the artillery attack by the HV was proper and directed towards military targets and not towards civilian targets. That particular report, along with its author, are the only hard evidence to come before this Court by the United Nations at the time. What is interesting to note is that this witness, this head of the military monitoring commission, has been removed from the witness list by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's not interesting to know but the Court knows that because there is litigation about that, Mr. Kehoe, so therefore --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I understand, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's be very practical. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, sir. And moving on practicalities and talking about the issue of that shelling. The Prosecution has made much that the shelling was designed to bring terror to the civilian population. What is not brought to your attention is the actual law in that regard, that the ICRC and their commentary on the protocols says that that is a natural consequence of a military attack and that attacks on armed forces are purposely conducted brutally in order to intimidate the enemy soldiers and to persuade them to surrender. Probably more important than anything else that was overlooked with regard to General Gotovina is that he was an operational commander, an operational commander that with his army was able to do that which no other army was able to do. In the midst of a time frame when the Bosnian Serb army with Ratko Mladic at its helm and President Karadzic running the Republika Srpska, the Bosnian Serbs were attempting to solidify their hold on the grounds gained and to connect the Krajina with the lands held by the Bosnian Serbs. There was one person, Mr. President and Your Honours, that brought the demise of the Bosnian Serb army and the end of the war in the former Yugoslavia, the one person at the head of those armies that brought the carnage in the former Yugoslavia from 1991 to 1995 to an end, one person, that man. At the direction of the HV and then in conjunction with the Bosnian Muslim army brought to heel that which international armies were never able to do. And what was also not brought to your attention was that Operation Storm was a series of plans that were -- that were designed to bring the Bosnian Serbs to heel. It started in summer of 1995 with taking of the high ground over Knin. It then moved to Operation Storm on the 1st, 4th, 5th of August. It then moved in September and October to Operation Maestral and Operation Southern Movement, all being directed by General Gotovina to finally defeat the Bosnian Serb army and bring them to the negotiating table and to put this carnage to an end. That is the man who sits before you. But I think, Your Honour -- Mr. President and Your Honours, in order to look to see how we got to 1995, it's important to take a look at what happened preceding that. As Your Honours know, and we're not here to rehash the history of the former Yugoslavia, by the time 1991 came around, Yugoslavia as it was post-Second World War was falling apart. In 1991 there were public referendums both in Slovenia and in Croatia declaring independence from the former Yugoslavia. That particular referendum in Croatia was on the 25th of June, 1991. Shortly thereafter, international recognition came to Croatia. And while the Yugoslavia as -- the prior Yugoslavia being run by Slobodan Milosevic and backed by the Yugoslav People's Army, the JNA, were not particularly interested in the Slovenians leaving, they were quite interested in keeping the Serbs in the former Yugoslavia. And so we -- what begins to evolve is the determination of or the evolution through the words and propaganda of Slobodan Milosevic of a Greater Serbia, that all Serbs will be able to live together in one state and that even though through public referendums within a democratic election in Croatia held in 1991 that the people decided to secede from the former Yugoslavia, such was not to be the case. Slobodan Milosevic was not allowed -- going to allow Croatia to leave with the Serb population that inhabited areas such as the Krajina, Eastern Slavonia, and in Western Slavonia which encompassed -- well, Eastern Slavonia, Vukovar, and Western Slovenia about midway through Croatia. And what was unleashed at that particular point was the JNA. The Yugoslav People's Army was unleashed on the Croats in order to bring them to heel, and what happened at that juncture is nothing short of horrific, and we'll show you in a moment exactly what happened in the wake of that attack. We had an army of the -- one of the most powerful armies in Europe unleashed on the civilian population in Croatia in order to bring them to heel. And one might ask why the Croats didn't fight back. The reality is, Your Honours and Mr. President, that in 1991, the Republic of Croatia had nothing with which to fight back. It was a new country with no army and no military and was pitting itself against one of the most powerful and largest armies in Europe, the Yugoslav People's Army. And in conjunction with this attack by the JNA, we have the formulation within the Republic of Serb Krajina of many of the individuals that you hear throughout this, Milan Martic, Milan Babic, Radovan Karadzic, and last but not least, General Mladic. Interestingly, going back as early as 1991 when the Republic of Serb Krajina was coming into its incipiency, was in its incipiency with Milan Martic at its head with Milan Babic, one of the members of the officers of the JNA that was supporting their tasks was none other than Ratko Mladic. And in the face of the democratically elected country, in June of 1991 the Republic of Serb Krajina declared its existence and independence in the summer of 1991. And with the assistance of the JNA solidified their gains both in the Krajina and in Eastern and Western Slavonia, so after a point almost a third of the Republic of Croatia was in the hands of the Serbs or the JNA. And what happened at the hands of the JNA was nothing short of horrific. One need only to look what happened to the beautiful town of Vukovar, a baroque city on the coast of the Danube to begin to understand the carnage that was inflicted on the Croatian population throughout the latter part of 1991 until the end of the war in -- in the end -- of the cease-fire in November of 1991. Let me show Your Honours and Mr. President a short piece of that carnage for Your Honours to understand, just a brief history of what this country had gone through in order to declare itself as a sovereign, if we may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: "As soon as the Slovenes and the Croats announced their independence Milosevic started the war. He bungled an attack on Slovenia but after the humiliation he turned his attention to Croatia. His military strategy consists of first bombarding his target from the air, then the troops pound the area with long-range missiles. After a while the tanks move in, followed by swarms of militiamen. "Terrible acts of brutality and looting have taken place within these homes. We see only the after-effects when nothing has been left worth a price on the black market. "Leaders of the European Union decided to send the British nominee Lord Carrington to intervene between what they called the warring factions. Diligently, he drew up one agreement after another for a cease-fire, each of which Milosevic eagerly signed and just as eagerly broke. "Nothing compared in horror to the siege of Vukovar. They wanted to rob them of their past, their history, their memories, their identity. They wanted to make it as if they had never existed. They burned their books, their archives, their records, their manuscripts, their registers of births and deaths, all in the name of ethnic cleansing. They smashed their ancient monuments, even their grave stones and their churches, always their churches, but they could not kill the spirit of the people of Vukovar. Against the cruelest of killing machines they held out day after day, night after night for as many as 90 days and nights. The Serbs boasted tomorrow Vukovar will fall, but the people would not surrender. No one came out of the cellars and begged for mercy. No one came out of cellars until the beautiful town of Vukovar was no more. "The Serbs crowed over their victory as if they had routed a force as heavily armed as themselves. "Despite all the evidence to the contrary, the Serbs often accused their victims of killing their own people. "It's not Croatian territory. It's the territory of Yugoslavia, and the fact is those Croatian forces, they are the ones who killed, strangled, and massacred the people who were living here. "They have killed all our friends, and we are not guilty. We didn't want the war. We only loved them. We don't kill them. We don't hate. We still don't hate. "The French called for more effective intervention. In response the United Nations Security Council imposed an arms embargo on all the republics of former Yugoslavia, but the Croats were virtually defenseless, while the federal army generals boasted that they had stockpiled enough to keep the war going for another six years. Their superior technology enabled them to conquer with the greatest of ease a third of Croatia. They also wrecked, wantonly and senselessly wrecked most of the show Serb villages within the Dubrovnik region "But everything depends on the cease-fire and after 12 cease-fires one cannot be very optimistic that it will hold. "Lord Carrington seems so unperturbed by the ceaseless breaking of cease-fires that the United Nations sent their own negotiator Cyrus Vance to see what he could do. He succeeded in establishing a temporary peace by endorsing the status quo. He brought in United Nations troops to guard the new frontier. This effectively prevented the Croats from retrieving their own territory. "Though Milosevic had lost the battle of Dubrovnik, he had cause for satisfaction. He had conquered a third of Croatia, wrecked its economy, killed over 9.000 people, made nearly a quarter of a million homeless, had smashed over 400 Catholic churches and had shown what he meant by ethnic cleansing, which is, of course, Fascism. "Questions were asked. Why couldn't the war be stopped? What was the purpose of NATO? The Americans threatened air-strikes and the bombing stopped, but it started again as soon as the threat was seen to be mere words. This is not and never was a civil war. It was mainly an unprovoked attack upon unarmed civilians by a heavily armed military force. It was genocide as President Izetbegovic always insisted. "How is it possible that we should have allowed such sights as these to be seen again in this century? "The heavily-armed secessionist Serbs easily concurred two-thirds of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The sight on our screens of the shelling of the bread queue, later the massacre in the marketplace of Sarajevo, shocked the world. Never were our leaders so contemptible as when they pretended not to know whether perhaps it had been the Muslims themselves who had been responsible for the massacre. "Again people asked why can't the war be stopped. Our leaders, having no policy of their own, could only respond to the public outcry. "[No interpretation]. "What does one say to the grown-up children of murdered parents? What does one say to them? How does one persuade the children of the Bosnians to accept European values when Europe is what has murdered their parents? How does one argue against the power of another ideology which is supplying them with guns? It's very hard to see. You know, if ten years from now, 15 years from now these kids have grown up and we find ourselves with an Hamas or a Hezbollah sitting on the edge of Western Europe and launching revenge attacks, revenge for the death of long-dead parents, what are we going to say to them? Do we say, you know, you are the terrorists? How can we call them terrorists when they have been so terrorised? "Our leaders have reneged on every relevant international agreement which they have signed on our behalf. Our leaders have closed their minds and hardened their hearts to the consequences of what they propose, a tolerance, almost an approval of a Fascist regime not far from our own doorsteps. Ghastly atrocities are at this moment being committed in the name of ethnic cleansing. "As for ourselves, how could we live with the shame of looking the other way?"

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, I want to show you that video --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, we asked ourselves why, because this Chamber's interested to hear the facts about the background of the conflict. Whether the Chamber's interested in what music has been chosen to underline pictures which we do not know to what extent it's journalistic material or whether it really represents what it says, of course the background of the conflict, atrocities committed elsewhere against Croats, against Muslims, et cetera, is certainly relevant. Let's keep it to facts. We are not a jury, and of course what the Chamber asked itself when looking at this video, whether in the exercise of the right of an accused to be tried in a public hearing, whether it was the public who was looking at how you addressed the Court or whether it was the Court that was allowed to observe how you address the public. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, the essence of this is how this all began, and in order to understand Operation Storm and what happened in its aftermath, it's essential to see what transpired prior to that and what happened throughout the evolution of this. What is also significant in this particular issue Vukovar, Your Honour, is that, and I will show you a short video of a comparison what happened in Vukovar and what happened in Knin, and I ask Your Honours and Mr. President to look at these facts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, I take it that the message was clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So therefore we don't have to compare who -- whom ill-treated, mistreated, because this Chamber, of course, follows not only what is now shown but of course has a lot of facts based on the case law of this Tribunal and of the case law in the republics of the former Yugoslavia where the Chamber is not presented a journalistic impression, and I have a question to you in relation to this, but can follow what has happened on the basis of evidence that was presented and that was challenged. I do not know whether this video will be later tendered into evidence and on what basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It will, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It will and then we will see whether there are any objections to that. Could you at least inform us at this moment what we looked at? Who broadcasted it, who --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The BBC. The prior, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: As the note had at the beginning of that, it was the British Broadcasting Corporation, the BBC.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: BBC. That's fine. Then we'll see what happens if this is tendered into evidence whether there's any objection against it then. But the Chamber is most assisted by, of course, giving the background, fine, but then to focus on what is at the core of this case. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And I would like to turn to a split screen comparison between Vukovar and Knin that we will also --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll look at it. I could split my screen and present whatever images. Let's look at it and see whether it assists --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- the Chamber. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It becomes clear to the Chamber what you're showing by a selection of pictures, that under the heading of Knin you showing buildings that are mainly intact and under Vukovar you present buildings that are heavily damaged.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If that is what you want the Court to understand, then you have succeeded and that it is the position of the Defence that whereas Knin, the buildings were not that much damaged. That was totally different in Vukovar. The Chamber has totally understood this. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, that the Office of the Prosecutor never charged an illegal shelling case for Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You know what it is. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I may, Judge, that one might ask how this happened, and as I referred to you before and this is significant towards the evolution of this case, because when we look back at 1991 there was no army of the Republic of Croatia. It was beginning to build. It was beginning to train, but they had nothing to fight the JNA. So the -- what happened after the Serbs and the JNA had solidified their gains in the Republic of Croatia was that the Vance Plan came in that was referred to in the video, and in January of 1992, and I have it back up on the screen, we see the areas in the map in orange that have been taken by the Serbs, both the Krajina Serbs and with the JNA, that then became UN protected areas and were solidified by the Vance Plan. So what the Vance Plan actually did in 1992 was to in fact solidify the gains of Serbs. Now, the design of that plan with the oncoming of UNPROFOR in 1992, was the United Nations, as the Martic judgement pooled, was designed to ensure that the areas remain demilitarised and that all persons residing in them were protected from fear of armed attack. Unfortunately, from 1992 until Operation Flash and Operation Storm, and in 1995, nothing could be further from the truth. If we turn our attention to the Special Rapporteur's report from 1994, paragraph 136, that's on the screen: "According to UNHCR statistics from 1994, 800-900 Croats, many of whom are elderly or disabled have remained in UNPAs, United Nations Protected Areas, Sector South. It is estimated that 44.000 Croats lived in the area before the conflict broke out in 1991. "Demographic estimates of UN protected area UNPA Sector North from 1994 indicate that, out of a total population of 112.000, 1.000 Croats and Muslims have remained despite earlier ethnic cleansing." Suffice it to say that the Vance Plan and its designs by the United Nations to protect both the Croat and the Muslim ethnic populations in their UN protected areas was a disaster. The reports of ethnic cleansing, killings, sufferings, and other injuries inflicted on the Croat and Muslim population from 1992 through 1995 are vast. This, this, in the face of the idea of the Vance Plan that these areas, including the Krajina, was still part of the Republic of Croatia. And suffice it to say during that entire period of time, there has been -- was no successful diplomatic effort to bring those areas back into the Republic of Croatia. So how did they fight back? What was the Republic of Croatia to do? What the Republic of Croatia did, luckily enough, was have people like Ante Gotovina come back, a man who had spent some time in the French Foreign Legion and in the military to come back to save the homeland, to begin to train the troops. General Gotovina had no background in traditional JNA doctrine that you saw inflicting injury on Vukovar. He came back in in 1991 and worked his way up through the various ranks in the Croatian army, taking the rank as a man who led from the front. Not a staff officer back in headquarters but a man who led from the front that showed his troops the way to go, and he rose to the top. Truly he had help. You will see during the course of this trial that the United States authorised the company called MPRI to come in with the Croatian army, to assist in the building of the Croatian army. General Gotovina set up an officers training school where international humanitarian law was taught. Those graduates of that academy graduated for the first time in 1994. Truly, truly an army that was growing right before his eyes. But throughout it all, Mr. President, Your Honours, it was a man, this was an officer --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, it's now approximately 25 times and when you talk about Mr. Gotovina that you turn your back to the Court and turn to Mr. Gotovina. If you address the Court, the Chamber by now, after 25 times, knows where Mr. Gotovina is seated. That's to our right. Therefore, again this is not a theatre. This is a court of law where a professional Bench hears your opening statement. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This is a man who has never lost sight of what he thought was right and wrong through leading his men in battle, Mr. President and Your Honours. And I would like to show you, Your Honour, a brief interview of an individual who will present himself to Mr. President and Your Honours concerning who General Gotovina was in the face of that battle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please play the video.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] At the time General Gotovina had only asked me to come but he didn't tell me there was an impending military operation called Maslenica, which was conducted five days after my meeting with the commissioned and non-commissioned officers in the Zadar hinterland. "General Gotovina certainly want me to set forth the Catholic principles regarding conduct in war. These issues interested both him and his associates who were present, so that through the lecture, the conference and the discussion which were held, I relayed the teachings of the Catholic church concerning the conduct of soldiers in a war in which they are defending their homeland in order to set forth the position on how to conduct oneself in military operations, in action, in military action, which was then imminent. I didn't know at the time. He didn't reveal to me why he had invited me, but I saw afterwards and later on in numerous conversations with the general we recalled this event. In later conversations, because he told me it was of great important to him that as a bishop, I set forth the Catholic teachings so that his commissioned and non-commissioned officers could abide by these Catholic teachings during war. We were taught during war one must remain ethical and that there are limits to legitimate defence which must not be crossed. "When discussing ethics in war and peace, I told the Croatian officers it was necessary to conduct a legitimate defence and that one must not go beyond the limits of legitimate defence, nor should one be destructive. I told them that it's not ethical to rape, to loot, or to commit any form of evil. Everything that is necessary in order to defend your country and which does not humiliate others, that is, that should be woven into military ethics, into the ethics of those who are at war. "My perception of General Gotovina judging from my meetings with him is a positive one. In my opinion, General Gotovina is a man who upheld war ethics and a man who said to me after I'd held the conference, 'Your Excellency, it is very important to me that you addressed my officers, my commissioned and non-commissioned officers, with those words which I shall repeat to them constantly so that they adhere to them.' "When I met General Gotovina after Operation Maslenica and later on during other operations, he would visit me as I told you for Christmas, Easter, and new year, and he told me that he kept my words in mind all the time."

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Suffice it to say, Mr. President and Your Honours, that when General Gotovina was instructing his troops, he was instructing his troops to act ethically, honourly, honestly, and morally. If we move ahead, Your Honour. Much had happened during this period of time between 1992 and 1995. Certainly, the rise of the Bosnian Serb army solidifying their gains in conjunction with the gains in Croatia were taking place. Diplomacy had failed on the international level throughout 1992, 1993 and 1994 with the Bosnian Serbs repelling the Vance-Owen Plan and also the Contact Group plan in 1994. I know Your Honours know much about that. But clearly the year 1995, after the international community had tired of the war in the former Yugoslavia, clearly that was the point at which the end game was going to come about. The Bosnian Serbs understood that they -- this was their time to solidify their territorial gains, and that is what they set out to do. The Republic of Srpska and the Republic of Serb Krajina commenced in 1995 to bring about that end game. In February of 1995, specifically 20 February, 1995, the Republic of Srpska and the Republic of Serb Krajina announced the formation of a joint defence council. They were henceforth formally operating together. In March of 1995, President Radovan Karadzic set forth his end game for the eastern enclaves of Srebrenica and Zepa, and we have it before the screen. "The first goal, such goal is the separation from the other two national communities. "The second strategic goal is the corridor between Semberija and Krajina ... there will be no Krajina, Bosnian Krajina or Serb Krajina or an alliance of Serbian states if we do not secure that corridor. "The sixth strategic goal is the access of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina to the sea." In a directive that was given in March of 1997 by Radovan Karadzic concerning the solidification of their goals in Srebrenica and Zepa, the Office of the Prosecutor has described it as such. Directive 7 directed the Bosnian Serb army to complete the physical separation of Srebrenica from Zepa as soon as possible, preventing even communication between individuals in the two enclaves. A planned and well-throughout combat operations create an unbearable situation of insecurity with no hope of further survival or life for the inhabitants of Srebrenica. That was in March of 1995. In May of 1995, the cease-fire expired, and May 26th of 1995, the Bosnian Serbs took UN peacekeepers hostage. As we move into July of 1995 given the state of affairs in the former Yugoslavia with no hope of bringing about a peaceful solution to this, the United Nations considered evacuating its peacekeepers. And then the final end game began with the attack on Srebrenica and Zepa in the first week of July of 1995. Unfortunately and tragically, as Mr. President and Your Honours know, the world stood by while more than 7.000 Bosnian Muslim men were taken out and executed. The response by the international community was virtually nothing. And let it not be said that that was the only theatre of operation that the Serbs were operating in at that time. As you can see on the map that is on the screen, the enclaves of Srebrenica and Zepa and thereafter Gorazde were under siege, and clearly as they moved to their end game to solidify their goals, they had to move to the circle that is number 1 up in the corner, which is the Bihac pocket. Now, Mr. President, I know you've heard quite a bit about the Bihac pocket. And, Your Honours, the Bihac pocket was an enclave, a Bosnian Muslim enclave, that was surrounded by the Bosnian Serbs. Why was it so important? It was important because with that fall or potential fall of Bihac the Bosnian Serbs, along with the Krajina Serbs, would be unified. The goal of a Greater Serbia would have been achieved, and the goal set forth by Radovan Karadzic that we talked about previously would have been brought about. It was essential that Bihac not fall. Why else was it essential for Bihac not to fall, because is there any doubt that if Bihac fell that the rivers of north-west Bosnia, like Srebrenica, would have run red with the blood of Bosnian Muslims at the hands at Ratko Mladic? I submit to you there is no doubt about that. And after the gains in Srebrenica and Zepa were solidified, the new Krajina Serb general, General Mrksic, began the move on Bihac and launched an attack on the 17th of July, on the 17th of July of 1995. What fear did that run through the international community? Ambassador Galbraith of the United States said the greatest evil was the possible fall of Bihac and the risk of the massacre of 40.000 people. And Ambassador Galbraith's testimony in the Milosevic case: "We were deeply concerned that Bihac would fall, that it would become another Srebrenica. It was four times as populous as Srebrenica, so we were concerned that we could see 30 to 40 thousand people being massacred if -- if Mladic and the Bosnian Serbs did the same thing." In his testimony in Martic, Ambassador Galbraith reiterated these comments. "In July of 1995 the Bosnian Serb had overrun Srebrenica, massacred some 7.000 men and boys, and had overrun another safe area, Zepa, and it, along the forces of the RSK, was launching an attack on Bihac that looked like it might prevail. This was intolerable for the Croatian government, as indeed was intolerable for the United States. The Croatians feared that if Bihac was overrun and -- that there would be another massacre, the survivors would end up in Croatia which already had been burdened by receiving some 2 million refugees passing through the country since 1991. That it would create a solid Western Serb entity of the RSK, plus the Bosnian Serb territory, so would put Croatia at a strategic disadvantage and the Croatian government was not going to let that happen. They saw that there was no prospect of successful peace negotiations with the Krajina Serbs, given the attitude of the accused who is Milan Martic, who refused to negotiate." In response the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Republic of Croatia met at Split in July of 1995, July 22nd, 1995. "And the agreement was to allow the Bosnian Serb to operate in conjunction with the army of the Republic of Croatia and to allow the HV to operate in Bosnia. You see, what was happening at this juncture was that RSK troops were moving from the Krajina into Bihac. And with the permission of the army -- excuse me, of the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina, General Gotovina led an attack on July the 27th in Grahovo to take the pressure off the Bihac pocket and to allow the Bihac pocket and the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina to survive. He led that attack commencing on the 26th of July and was successful by the 27th of July. And, Mr. President and Your Honours, it worked. There was a withdrawal from the attack on Bihac at that time, and Bihac did not fall. The Bosnian Serbs in conjunction with the army of the Serb Krajina were unsuccessful in taking that. Nevertheless, notwithstanding the loss of Grahovo, Milan Martic, then the president of the Republic of Serb Krajina, had no desire to live in a Republic of Croatia in peace, had no desire to engage in any negotiation to bring about a peaceful resolution of this, and we hear as much in a conversation that he had in Knin shortly after the fall of Grahovo in the 27th of July.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] Nobody has the right to stop halfway and to reconsider whether we could have lived with our demons. It is clear that such a life is impossible, and for this reason we are keeping only one thing in mine. We haven't been offered any possibility of peace. We aren't in a position to choose peace. We are being offered slavery, a life of uncertainty and a fight for freedom. And with regards to this choice, I'm fully committed towards the fact that we have to fight to the end in our fight for freedom. We need to bear in mind only one thing: How to remain strong in a military sense and capable of defending ourselves. After having repeated the opinion that the Republic of Srpska Krajina should never be a part of Croatia, President Martic especially stressed the conviction that the Serb people have the strength to endure that honourable fight for their existence to be fought until the very end and to show the demons that the Republic of Srpska Krajina was and will remain Serb ethnic territory."

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And to solidify that, Your Honour, what the -- I'm sorry, Your Honour. And to solidify that, Your Honour, what the Bosnian Serbs and the Krajina Serbs were doing was preparing for war. If we could turn our attention to the video of 18, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: "The Bosnian Serbs and their allies -- crisis meetings not because America has moved one step closer to lifting the arms embargo and not because NATO is threatening robust action to protect the remaining safe areas. It is the prospect of an all-out conflict with the Croatian army that prompted this council of war. The Bosnian Serb military commander General Ratko Mladic meeting rebel Serb commanders from Croatia to plan a joint strategy. The military council meeting --"

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: But as this was going on -- I'm sorry, Your Honour. I apologise, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm -- I'm following the translation, and if you take a little break so that they can finish the French translation then please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. While the Bosnian Serbs and the Krajina Serbs were preparing for war, they are also trying to give the view in buying time through some efforts or supposed efforts on their part at diplomacy and we had a series of meetings that were going on in Geneva in the first few days of August. Well, what is clear, what is clear from this, in this particular tape of the 2nd of August, 1995, was that Martic had no intention whatsoever of engaging in any peace negotiations. If we look at the centre of that page when they are talking about a Z-4 plan and the Z-4 plan was the plan being proposed by Ambassador Galbraith which, among other details, allowed for the peaceful reintegration of the Krajina Serbs into the Republic of Croatia. Prijic, the individual says: They are dispersed there but we cannot accept the Z-4 plan. "Martic: Out of the question. Out of the question. There will be no discussions about the Vance Plan or about Z-4." They have no interest whatsoever in engaging in this. What they are engaged in, Your Honours, is a plan for war. This is all within a few days of each other, Your Honour, and I will turn our attention to exactly one last item which is the BBC broadcasting reflection of a radio Knin -- a radio Knin broadcast. And about midway down --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You have to slow down for the --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- interpreters. Perhaps if you repeat your last few sentences.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. What we have on the screen before us is an article that comes from a BBC world report concerning the negotiations in Geneva. And suffice it to say from this article, and we need not go into it in detail, is that Prijic and the Krajina Serbs have no interest whatsoever in negotiating a peaceful resolution. And coming until the first few days in August with this intercept and the other information coming from the Krajina Serbs, President Tudjman, General Gotovina, and others know it. The only thing that they are doing is buying time, and buying time and preparing for war. And the person that is going to lead that war in conjunction with the General Mrksic is none other than Ratko Mladic. And then on July 30th of 1995, General Mladic comes to Knin to discuss that matter. If we can turn to the videotape.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] General Ratko Mladic, the legendary commander of the Main Staff of the Republika Srpska army, an old acquaintance and one of the Serb legends. "So this is an opportunity to use the presence of General Mladic to address you and to ask him questions concerning the current situation which is of great importance to the Serb people, critical. So I now give the floor to General Mladic and will not be taking up any more of your time. So, Mr. General, please go ahead. "Thank you very much. If I could I would like to take this opportunity to use the media in order to address the people, to greet the people of the Republic of Srpska Krajina. We are here together. I've always been here even if I left and was away for a while. I never really left here. "Maybe for starters Mr. General how do you perceive the situation as a whole in the Republic of Srpska and the Republic of Srpska Krajina? "Currently, I would say that the situation is quite complex due to an extensive aggression being conducted by the Croatian armed forces against the Republika Srpska. The goal of their operation being to cut off the Republic of Srpska Krajina and to use their weapons and the assistance of mediators and pressure by the international community to enforce a solution in the area by means of force. I do have a hope that with the help of good organisation and the function of all segments of the Serb people in both the Republika Srpska and the Republic of Srpska Krajina the outcome will be a successful one. I think the Croats have made a crucial mistake in this war and it is going to cost them dearly. "Do the Serbs have enough strength to withstand the Muslims and the Croats? "The Serb people have enough forces and sufficient strength and had countries from the German and Islamic bloc not provided support, unfortunately along with the support of some others, they would have lost this war long ago. Any prolongation of this war is disastrous, first of all for those who started, and here I mean the Croatian armed formations. "Mr. General, from a strategic point of view, in my humble opinion, I think the Croat forces are quite stretched across the territory now and towards the defence lines of our Serb defence forces. To what extent with respect to our strategy can this be -- can this be a fuse for a successful strategic strike to retake and liberate our territories? "I won't address this question. You pose a good question taking into consideration the fact that you express typical journalist curiosity. I wouldn't answer your question with any particularly high degree of precision. Time will show and time will answer your question. "Mr. General, what is the current situation in the Grahovo and Glamoc battlefields. "Croatia's military formations have carried out attacks, entered Grahovo and in part Glamoc as well. I do hope that we will retake these and other occupied territories of the Republic of Srpska very soon. "Among other issues we are interested in the situation in Grahovo and Glamoc in the area of responsibility of the 2nd Krajina Corps. All sorts of rumours are being circulated among the public, even by some public information agencies in the Serb territories. There is insufficient defence coordination between the Republic of Srpska Krajina and Republika Srpska there are even rumours and attempts to stir unrest among the population. There are talks of some sorts of selling out or surrender of our liberated lands for a greater gain. "First of all, I won't be getting to commenting on this calculated propaganda, low intensity propaganda. As far as I'm concerned the Serb population is unified from Kupa to Korana and all the way to Timok and South Morava. I feel that the Serb people in those territories, as should a lot of people on the planet, have the same interests, the same state and remaining structures of such a state. And I believe that with regard to that, what is going on in every part of those territories, needless to say, is with every individual on the planet that Serbs should be allowed to demonstrate an interest in at least the same degree as any other modern state demonstrates for its citizens living within their state or in foreign territory. "Surprised you by his presence but this doesn't mean that they have asked me many questions up to now and they know what I think [inaudible]. "You posed a good question. This isn't the first time the Ustasha formations attacked our lives. "That was a good question. This isn't the first time the Ustasha formations attacked our lives. However, I believe the time has come that our people as a whole realised something that many have come to realise during this war and something that I have been indicating all along. I believe terrible mistakes were made by individuals who claimed the war with the Croats was over once for all or that it would be over within seven days and that in the lines, along the lines of separation, numerous check-points were being opened, customs zones. In some places there were even soccer games being held. As you can see, these proved to be costly decisions resulting in the loss of lives, numerous refugees and burned villages, but I hope our people have now understood this and they have enough strength, they will muster enough strength so that this aggression by Croatia by has been present with its armed force during the whole time of this war in the whole territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina be avenged and so that we send them back to where they belong, their own territory. "I just want to send my regards to the people. I want to tell them they should remain resolute in defending their century-old historical hearth and graves and not to give into any acts of provocation or any form of propaganda because it is only with the means of our forces that we are creating our state. A state can be made only by using one's own children and so many of our wonderful children have given their lives for both the Republic of Srpska Krajina and the Republika Srpska which should motivate the rest of us who are still alive and on our feet to apply additional efforts and that we remain focused on the final stage of this war. Until the final victory. That's right. "Thank you very much."

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So Your Honours, quite clearly from this -- I'm sorry, Your Honour, I don't know if the French translation was finished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes. Quite clearly from this interview in Knin during this period of time they are getting prepared for one thing and one thing only which is to bring about the final solidification of their territorial gains. And how were they going to do that? In what fashion were they going to do that? Were they going to taste the Bihac pocket and other lands taken by the army of the Republic of Croatia in a fashion in accordance with international humanitarian law or were they going to use the tasks and methods employed in Srebrenica and Zepa? Ratko Mladic answers that himself.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] Mr. General, will the Muslims from Bihac continue to provoke the Serb defence in the area of Ribic and thereon much longer?" "Yes. And they will until they have been completed defeated as they were in Srebrenica and Zepa."

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: As they were defeated in Srebrenica and Zepa. There is no doubt what would happen if General Gotovina and the HV had not ensured that the Bihac pocket would not fall. Had he not come forward and began not only summer 1995 which was the taking of Grahovo, but then Operation Storm in August of 1995 followed by Operation Maestral and followed by Operation Southern Movement. General Gotovina and the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina changed the entire international landscape to bring about the defeat of the Bosnian Serbs and to end this carnage once and for all. And those words are not necessarily mine. They are the words of negotiators on behalf of the United States and the international community and also the president of the United States. He we turn to the book on the screen. This was an excerpt from the book written by President Clinton, his memoirs, where he writes at the bottom of the page: "In August, the situation took a dramatic turn. The Croats launched an offensive to retake the Krajina, a part of Croatia that the local Serbs," we are moving to the top of the next page, "had proclaimed their territory. European and some military and intelligence officials had recommended against the action in the belief that Milosevic would intervene to save the Krajina Serbs, but I was rooting for the Croatians. So was Helmut Kohl, who knew, as I did, that diplomacy could not succeed until the Serbs had sustained some serious losses on the ground. "Because we knew Bosnia's survival was at stake, we had not tightly enforced the arms embargo. As a result, both the Croatians and the Bosnians were able to get some arms which helped them survive. We had also authorised a private company to use retired US military personnel to improve and train the Bosnian Serb army," -- excuse me, "the Croatian army." The key, Your Honour, is in the last sentence of the paragraph before that diplomacy could not succeed until the Serbs had sustained some serious losses on the ground. That idea was echoed by Richard Holbrooke where he noted, I'm quoting one of his colleagues: "I realise how much the Croatian offensive in the Krajina profoundly changed the nature of the Balkan game and thus this diplomatic offensive." General Wesley Clark simply called it the turning point. Mr. President and Your Honours, we are now going to -- I'm going to turn this over to my colleague, Mr. Misetic, to talk yet further about Operation Storm in some degree of detail, but I want to end, Your Honours, with this one last point before the break: The man who brought about the turning point, Mr. President and Your Honours, the man who brought this war and this carnage to an end sits before you. The man who, if anyone is responsible for peace and bringing an end to the war in the former Yugoslavia, is General Ante Gotovina. That is the man before you with which I hope this Court, Mr. President and Your Honours, gives full breadth and full consideration when we are revealing the facts before us. If time permits, I may have some concluding arguments, but if not, I yield the floor to my colleague, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, before you start, how much time you would need? I have to find out whether it would be more suitable to take a break now or after you've started.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I think a break would be appropriate now, Your Honour. I have a significant portion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Kehoe, I have one question that -- for you at this very moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You spent a lot of time on what caused the military operations in the summer of 1995, and you spent a lot of time on explaining what the positive effect would be and to what extent it was justified to take such action. Now, I might have misunderstood Mr. Tieger yesterday, but I think in five lines explained to us that he did not challenge the right of the Republic of Croatia to retake the area that was earlier taken by the Serbs so that the mere fact that retaking and bringing back to its internationally recognised boundaries was, as far as I understand, not contested as legitimate by the Prosecution. So therefore I asked myself a couple of times what actually in this respect keeps the parties apart.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm glad you asked that question, Your Honour, without getting into the law on this regard but I think it's important that we ascertain the distinction between an operational commander and one who is a functional military governor or responsible for matters in his flank. And I direct Your Honour to the high command case where General von Leeb, while there was ethnic cleansing going on with various groups coming out of the SSS who were attached to General von Leeb, the Court noted that General von Leeb was an operational commander. He was responsible for offensive operations. And it is -- what is significant and very, very important to this case, Your Honour, is for us to explain to Mr. President and Your Honours the role of an operational commander and what he is tasked to do. And what he was tasked to do was to bring about the defeat of the Bosnian Serb army and also the army of the Republic of Serb Krajina. That being said, his responsibility vis-a-vis -- vis-a-vis taking care of things that are 250 kilometres in his flank is non-existent. Even if the -- von Leeb said even if he had the potential right to intervene, he did not have direct responsibility. So what was important for the Defence of General Gotovina, Mr. President, was to circumscribe and explain that he was truly an operational commander operating in the offensive with the design to bring about the defeat of the Serbs in various theatres not only in the Krajina but in Bosnia-Herzegovina. It is a matter of law that these facts will apply to, and I refer back to the High Command case which the Celebici Appeals Chamber cited with authority. Now, with that in mind, Judge, tasking what an operational commander is doing and how he is operating is highly, highly significant to the defence of General Gotovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I still do not know whether in many respects there is disagreement between the parties in this respect, but we'll then further hear about that. We'll have a break and we'll resume at a quarter to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, before I allow you to continue, I'd like to put on the record that the Chamber is aware that now and then where reference is made to Mr. Martic, the transcript, at least the provisional transcript, reads Markac, and that's of course a mistake. It will be corrected anyhow, but the Chamber, if only from the context, perfectly well understood when the reference was made to Mr. Martic. Mr. Misetic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President and Your Honours, may it please the Court, Judge Schomburg of the Appeals Chamber once remarked in an interview concerning some of the indictments before the ICTY he said: "What is particularly critical is the mostly vague indictments. They often comprise a stockpile of a whole range of possible actions and their implementation. One can't help getting the impression that an arrest warrant is issued first and only afterwards do the actual investigations begin." This case at the end of the -- at the conclusion of the Prosecution's evidence is a perfect example of what Judge Schomburg was referring to. At the end of the Prosecution's case in chief, you, too, will come to the same conclusion. There is no evidence to support the Prosecution's charges against General Gotovina, and there never has been. A Franciscan friar named William of Ockham who was a 14th Century logician is the author of a principle of logic that has become famously known as Occam's principle or Occam's Razor. Occam's Razor paraphrased states that: All other things being equal, the simplest answer is the best. Throughout this trial, the Prosecution will consistently and repeatedly ask you to violate Occam's principle. To reject the simple, straightforward interpretation of the evidence in favour of a tenuous, complicated conspiracy theory. Their entire case literally rests on your willingness to believe the conspiracy theory despite the overwhelming evidence that refutes that very theory. For example, the Prosecution will ask you to believe that Operation Storm was a vast joint criminal enterprise designed to ethnically cleanse the Serbian population from Croatia. This is wholly without merit. The simple straightforward answer is that Operation Storm was launched with the best of intentions, to end Milosevic's, Karadzic's Mladic's, and Martic's four year reign of terror in Croatia and Bosnia and to do it while protecting the safety and security of the Serb population which would remain in Croatia. It had the blessings of portions of the international community specifically the United States of America and President Clinton, provided that certain conditions were met. The evidence in this case will show that the Croatian government, including the Croatian army, planned and executed Operation Storm so as to minimise civilian casualties and to provide safety and security to those Serbs that remained in Croatia. The Prosecution points to the Brioni meeting as an alleged meeting where criminal conspiracy was hatched. Nothing could be further from the truth. The Brioni meeting was a meeting where the Croatians discussed -- the Croatian government discussed destroying a criminal conspiracy, Martic's and Milosevic's criminal conspiracy. At no point during the Brioni meeting does President Tudjman suggest to those present that they should force Serb civilians to flee. Show 23A, please. In the Martic case, the Prosecution submitted both pre-trial and final trial briefs and here are some of the excerpts of the Prosecution's position as recently as 14 months ago in the Martic case. I quote: "The implementation of this plan (referring to Martic's joint criminal enterprise) took several forms. An intense media campaign directed by members of the Martic JCE in Belgrade began to portray Serbs in Croatia as being discriminated against and victimised by the Croat majority and imminently threatened with genocide by the latter. "This threat, which was repeatedly echoed by Martic and other Serb nationalist leaders in Croatia, Bosnia and Herzegovina and Belgrade, instilled fear and resentment in the Serb population and eliminated the possibility of co-existence between the ethnic groups. "As a result of the implementation of this criminal plan, Serbs living in Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina were made to believe that they could only feel safe in a homogeneous Serbian state." And then in the final trial brief --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, I hear the French interpreters struggling with your speed of speech. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Sorry. The Prosecution 14 months ago told the Trial Chamber in the Martic case: "There is no evidence that Croatian leaders or the Croatian media were actually threatening the Serbs with genocide, as claimed by Serb leaders at the time." This was the Prosecution's case in Martic. The Prosecution said Martic's intense propaganda over four years had "eliminated the possibility of co-existence with the Croats." That the Serbs were made by Martic to believe that they could "only feel safe in a homogeneous Serbian state." That the Croatian government -- there is no evidence that the Croatian government was actually threatening the Serbs with genocide. President Tudjman, in planning Operation Storm understood that Serb civilians had become victims of Milan Martic's propaganda campaign for four years and that they had been made to believe that they could not live in a Croatian state. As a result, prior to Operation Storm, it was understood not only by President Tudjman but by the entire international community that if Croatia were compelled by Milan Martic to use force to retake its occupied territories, many Serb civilians would flee as a result of the fear of Croatia that had been ingrained in them by Martic. What is the evidence for what I have just told you? Well, the evidence, Your Honours, is as the Prosecution made reference yesterday to an operation of the Croatian army known as Operation Flash in May of 1995. During Operation Flash, Croatia recovered its territory in Western Slavonia. Many Serbs fled Western Slavonia when the Croatian forces launched the operation. However, some Serbs stayed behind. At the insistence of Mr. Martic, the United Nations organised a programme to take out the remaining Serbs from Western Slavonia and to move them to Banja Luka. The UN Special Rapporteur for Human Rights submitted a report on this topic in July -- 5 July 1995, which is on your screens, and he wrote, paragraph 29 -- sorry, paragraph 28, please. "During the first two days of the military operation, as many as 10.000 people fled from the Serb-held area of Western Slavonia, mostly from the Okucani area, across the Sava River bridge into northern Bosnia ... the RSK authorities had previously held regular evacuation drills, and there were reports that some of the refugees may have been forced into leaving against their will. Subsequently, in negotiations with the United Nations Protection Force and Croatian authorities, the leaders of the RSK insisted that the persons left behind, estimated at 3 to 4.000, be given the opportunity to leave Western Slavonia and join the other refugees in the Serb-held territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The United Nations acceded to this demand and initiated the programme known as Operation Safe Passage with the context of the four point Cessation of Hostilities Agreement. 29: "Serbs still living in the sector were advised of their right to remain and the public assurances of the government of Croatia that their rights, including the right to citizenship of the Republic of Croatia, would be fully respected. Nevertheless, during the month of May hundreds of Serbs from Sector West applied for inclusion in Operation Safe Passage and by early June more than 2.000 had left for Serb-held territory in Bosnia and Herzegovina. According to recent information, no more than 1.000 remain in the sector. Numerous observers have voiced concerns that the operation was conducted in an unduly hasty manner and persons were not adequately informed of their rights. However, continuing demand for inclusion in the exit convoys as late as mid-June suggests that most Serbs in Western Slavonia were intent upon leaving under any circumstances. Intending refugees interviewed by the Special Rapporteur's field office indicated that the main reasons for their wish to depart were the desire to join relatives who had already fled, and doubts about future prospects in Croatia, especially the security situation and the likelihood of finding work." This all took place, Your Honours, between 60 and 90 days before Operation Storm. The United Nations and international governments were certainly aware of the policies of Martic to have Serb civilians removed from areas where the Krajina Serb authorities did not control the territory. Who else in the international community knew that the Serb policies of Martic would result in the departure of the Krajina Serbs? Ambassador Peter Galbraith, the United States ambassador, in his diplomatic diary, entry on June 15th, six weeks before Operation Storm, wrote the following -- he talks -- the bottom paragraph. "If Croatia took the territory," he's referring to Sectors North and South, "the Krajina Serbs would leave. They could be resettled in Sector East thus threatening Milosevic's claim to territory that he very much wants for Greater Serbia." We don't only have Ambassador Galbraith's diary. Ambassador Galbraith tried to avoid conflict, tried to get the Krajina Serbs to come to their senses and agree to the peaceful reintegration of the so-called Krajina into Croatia, and so on the 2nd of August, he went to Belgrade and met with Milan Babic to try to convince him to accept the Z-4 plan. On the 3rd of August, Ambassador Galbraith, on the evening before Operation Storm, reported to Mr. Tudjman what he had discussed with Mr. Babic in Belgrade, and you will now hear the audio of Mr. Galbraith's conversation with President Tudjman and how he told Babic: "If you fail to agree to peace, the majority of Krajina Serbs will leave." Here is that audio:

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: "Mr. President, I have a -- I would like to report, if I may, on my meeting with Babic in Belgrade and that I have a message for you from our government which follows through on that meeting. But first on the meeting. "Babic had indicated he wished to see me, and since I'm not very popular in Knin after attending the Split meeting and after what I said about the attacks on Zagreb, he proposed the American embassy in Belgrade, and the administration, I made them aware of your subsequent concern that maybe it wouldn't be a good idea but they asked that I go anyhow. "He -- we met at the embassy in Belgrade. He came by himself. I began the meeting and I explained to him the facts of life as I saw them, namely that Croatia was poised to take military action to recover the entire Krajina. Well, anyhow by that I mean sectors north and south. That their action in going to Bihac had meant that they had forfeited a very significant international sympathy, that it was our judgement that if the Croatian army went it would be successful. And I said that this would be a great tragedy because we know that many of the Serbs who live there would leave, probably most of them. There would, of course, be thousands of dead on both sides."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That's an excerpt.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note that they did not have the transcript of this audio. It is not a custom to interpret if we don't have the audio, the transcript of the audio.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'll try to take care of that later for them, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That cannot, of course, undo what has happened already. Is there any audio or video clip to be played for which there is no written transcript available for the interpreters' booth?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: My case manager says we did e-mail it to them so I'm not sure -- except for this audio but for the rest we did. I would note, Your Honours, just one point there was an English translation prepared of this transcript by OTP but however, for whatever reason, this sentence where Mr. Galbraith says, "It would be a great tragedy. We know that many of the Serbs who live there would leave, probably most of them," for whatever reason was not translated. So that sentence was deleted in the English translation and I didn't have time to prepare a new translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm a bit surprised about an English translation, because I heard the text spoken in English, so what was there still translation from English into -- I'm a bit puzzled about your remark because why translate --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: She said she wanted a transcript. I thought she meant a transcript of the English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So it's not -- you say there was a transcript prepared in English which was not complete.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not a translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: A translation because there is a Croatian transcript of this that was translated by OTP. We got the English translation of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm really puzzled. I hear words spoken in English. I take it then that someone has translated it into Croatian or B/C/S, , whatever you'd like to call it, and then to translate it back when the original is available in English surprises me. So therefore I can imagine that a transcript of the words spoken is not available.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'll clarify. I don't believe that the OTP has this audio so it was never translated -- or transcribed, let me say, this way. They have a written transcript from the Croatian archives, from Croatian that they translated into English. The English translation of the written Croatian transcript did not have this sentence which is the need of why I had to use the audio which OTP doesn't have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now I better understand what the -- what happened and why it still was a translation. For the interpreters' booth, this will not happen again from what I understand from Mr. Misetic. Is there any need at this moment to repeat or to -- or were you able to follow the text in such a way that we can rely upon the translation as we find them on the transcript?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note it's fine, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your understanding. Then please proceed, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. So we see, Your Honours, that there was a whole record of knowledge prior to Operation Storm that the Serbs would leave. There's also more evidence. The Krajina Serb leadership on Krajina Serb television in July of 1995, weeks before Operation Storm, broadcast evacuation drills and their messages to the population. We have that video as well which we'd like to show you about how the Krajina Serb leadership was instilling fear in its own population and telling them to leave in the event of armed conflict.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] Having heard the sound of sirens we hurried towards Terzic. It is now five minutes to 6.00. We're located on a bridge crossing the river Mreznica, between Terzic and Primisalj. We encountered the commander of the 13th Infantry Brigade, Colonel Marko Reljic. As we speak, a column of civilians with vehicles and livestock are arriving from Terzic. What does this mean, commander? "Well, this is an exercise which we're conducting in accordance with our assumptions and our information that the enemy aviation will be active in this region using rockets and artillery and before this happens we have to evacuate, that is evacuate the civilian population from the combat area and our units will complete the tasks that they have been given. That means it is of importance to us to train the population, the civilian population to evacuate as to suffer as little losses as possible. "Are you satisfied with the exercise up to now? Are members of the 13th Infantry Brigade engaged in this exercise or are they manning their positions? "Members of the 13th Infantry Brigade are manning their positions and according to the tasks that they have received, all soldiers are at their positions. And I am very pleased with the conduct of the civilian population. They understand the situation and are aware of the fact that we need to prepare and be trained if we truly find ourselves in a situation to have to evacuate so that there are no unnecessary victims. And so that what happened in Western Slavonia does not happen to us again. "Absolutely. Thank you very much. "You're welcome. "Because Terzic is our first position which will be targeted so we wanted to test this and by means of this exercise we have to review whether we are well prepared, whether we are well-organised and what would be the best way to do this so as to avoid civilian victims should there be military activity. We need to evacuate the civilian population in due time. After having learned a lesson in Western Slavonia and throughout history and wars, the population needs to be evacuated and removed in time. The units and the army are to remain in their positions executing their tasks. It is extremely important that you understand and that you know that within your homes and families you need to prepare yourselves, organise yourselves, and upon receipt of the signal you need to withdraw to the designated region because the enemy wants to slaughter, to murder, to burn, to slaughter these children. That is why every citizen must be prepared for the evacuation. This evacuation won't be signalled in advance. There won't be enough time to prepare. You might have to [inaudible] they will have to save their skin. You must be prepared for this."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, we submit to you that the evidence at trial is going to be overwhelming that the Krajina Serb leadership, specifically Martic and his joint criminal enterprise, consistently and repeatedly used their civilian population as a tool in furtherance of the desire for Greater Serbia, that they instructed their civilian population both in Western Slavonia and immediately prior to Operation Storm through television broadcasts to "be ready to go when the desired signal is given." This was not a tactic that was limited to Mr. Martic. This was a tactic that was common to all of Milosevic's joint criminal enterprise. Indeed, it was well-known in the international community, and in 1999, when conflict again broke out in Kosovo, what did the international community assume would happen when international forces enter Kosovo? We have that as well. This is the Pentagon spokesman four days before NATO enters Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: "To keep hunting rifles and things like that which is different from complete disarmament, but -- "[Inaudible]. "There will be some sort of -- some sort of decision made about probably classifying weapons by calibre and I don't know what that is, but the issue is that there will not be anybody to fight. NATO's going to be there. NATO is going to be maintaining a secure environment. There's going to be a security border around Kosovo that will mean that the Serb troops have to be 25 kilometres away from the border with Kosovo, and I would expect that everybody will do what -- what they want to do, which is to rebuild their lives, to get home, to plant crops, to get their kids in school, to reunify their families, and that's the point of why NATO's going in to set up a stable environment. "As I understand it, it's 5 kilometres for the forces. "Can I just ask for a quick -- do you have any concerns about Kosovar Albanians or KLA's retaining their small arms and engaging in small arms fights with paramilitaries who may remain and NATO getting caught in the crossfire? "We always have to be concerned about threats to NATO troops. The fact of the matter is that I don't think that Kosovo is going to be a very happy place for Serbs when NATO comes in, and the -- and the -- I don't think Serbs will want to stay there. I think they will want to return to Serbia. I don't anticipate that's what's going to happen. I anticipate people will want to get home and rebuild their lives and that's what they'll devote their energies to. "[Indiscernible] said that 'Kosovo won't be a very happy place for Serbs.' "Well, I mean the Serb minority will be allowed to stay if it wants to stay. We're already getting some reports and suggestions that is most Serbs will want to go. We don't know how big the Serb minority is there; it's probably about a hundred thousand, could be a little more than that. But as Kosovar Albanians flow back in, our assumption is that many Serbs will probably return to Serbia "It sounds like you're encouraging the Serbs who now live in Kosovo then to leave. "I'm not encouraging them at all, I'm just stating what we anticipate the facts will be."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: What we anticipate the facts will be. Why is this relevant? Let's go back to the Brioni transcript. You have heard, Your Honours, the evidence of what was common knowledge prior to the Brioni meeting and prior to Operation Storm and indeed what became common knowledge after Operation Storm. On the Brioni transcript you will not find a single instance where President Tudjman encourages his generals to do something to cause Serb civilians to flee. Why? Because he didn't have to. There was no reason to force civilians to flee when it was common knowledge that the Serb leadership had as a policy that they were going to evacuate their civilians. Mr. Tieger cited the following quote from page 2 of that transcript. He says: "In which way do we resolve it? This is the subject of our discussion today. We have to inflict such blows that the Serbs will to all practical purposes disappear, that is to say, that the areas we do not take at once must capitulate within a few days." Your Honour, we submit that the proper interpretation when President Tudjman says "Serbs," he's not referring to Serb civilians, he's using the colloquial in the same way that we might say for US forces the Americans or the Germans or the Japanese, something to that effect, and we know that because in the highlighted area, the second highlight, he repeats the exact same thought. "Therefore, our main task is not Bihac, but instead to inflict such powerful blows in several directions that the Serbian forces will no longer be able to recover, but will have to capitulate." "Capitulate," the same word he used in the first paragraph. Armies capitulate, civilians don't capitulate. He's not talking about Serb civilians. Page 3. As to this issue that the Prosecution is going to attempt to put forward to you that Knin was undefended, what did the Croatians know: "Mr. President: Listen. How can they undertake a counter-attack against -- "Admiral Domazet: A counter-attack is two-fold, Mr. President. From Knin, or rather, to the northeast of Knin there are forces the adversary has partially transferred. The counter-attack forces come from two operational axes of Knin." The Croatian army did not anticipate that Knin would be undefended and in the fact Knin was not undefended and the evidence will be clear on that point at trial. Page 10. What is President Tudjman talking about on -- on the Brioni transcript? He is not -- he is not referring to an effort to force civilians to flee. Instead, in this passage you see President Tudjman is criticising the planning of Operation Storm because it left no exit route for the civilians who are anticipated to be prepared to flee for the reasons I've already spelled out, and in effect the plan initially drawn up was to trap the civilians and the military forces in the so-called Krajina. So the president says: "Do you know what, from a strategic point of view, is a drawback to our consideration of the plan? It's all very well that the Admiral is now supposed to close off their remaining three exits, but you are not providing them with an exit anywhere. There is no way out. (To close it off.) To pull out and flee; instead, you are forcing them to fight to the bitter end, which exacts a greater engagement and greater losses on our side." "Accordingly, let us take into consideration on a military level the possibility of leaving them a way out somewhere so they can pull out part of their forces ..." I understand. I apologise, Your Honour. I'll slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please. Yes, especially when you're reading. It's good to be aware that speed of speech usually goes up. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The issue of greater panic. When the president refers in the following statement, he says: " ... when we undertake a general offensive in the area even greater panic will break out in Knin." He does not say when we excessively shell or otherwise terrorise civilians, he is saying when we launch the operation and put pressure on their front lines, the plans put in place by the Krajina Serb leadership will cause panic, not that the Croatian forces are doing anything that is not in accordance with the laws of war. The president in a passage quoted by Mr. Tieger quotes the words where he -- President Tudjman talks about shelling for complete demoralisation.
