We will get to that in a few minutes and I will address that question. The president: "Is an attack on Knin possible without hitting the camp which UNCRO UNPROFOR has there? "General Gotovina: At this moment we can engage in extremely precise operations at Knin systematically without aiming at the barracks in which UNCRO is located. "Domazet: In those southern barracks, and his forces are to the north therefore we can fire with great precision without coming in the line of fire ..." Your Honours, think about what Admiral Domazet is saying there. The UNCRO camp will not be hit because it is in the sought of Knin and we are targeting the military barracks of the RSK forces which is in the north and therefore nothing will come in the line of fire. There's no discussion about spraying Knin with artillery shells at all. Finally, the general in the Croatian army in charge of logistics is named Vladimir Zagorec. General Zagorec is asked to comment on the state of the ammunition reserves and he says: "We can extend logistical support to one part. You have the inventory. However, the amount of ammunition used up at Glamoc and Bosansko Grahovo was relatively large. I am now only interested in this and I urge all commanders to take into account the amount of ammunition expended in these operations. We have reserves for some five days. However, attention should be paid to artillery." And then it goes on. And how does the president respond to this? How does he conclude the discussion about artillery? "Gentlemen, I said this to all of you and especially to some generals, that in this war we are really using up ammunition as if we were Russians or Americans. Therefore, use smaller units, engage in sabotage operations and use surprise. Strike with smaller infantry forces and even helicopter assaults where they are unexpected but where a far greater impact can be achieved - it is clear. If we had enough, then I, too, would be in favour of destroying everything by shelling prior to advancing." The sentiment is clear. "We don't have enough artillery, so don't waste it." Let me just note that there was a discussion about leaflets and I believe Mr. Tieger made a misstatement of fact. He stated that leaflets were dropped in Operation Storm prior to Martic issuing his evacuation order. And as you will see at trial, leaflets were dropped seven hours after Martic issues his evacuation order and the only thing the leaflet said was that the evacuation orders had been issued and here are the safe routes you can take to exit. Moving on from the Brioni meeting. It's also important to note something that the Prosecution did not discuss with you yesterday. High-level officials of the Croatian government travelled to Washington on the 1st of August. During that discussion, they received approval in the way that we would understand approval. I won't get into the diplomatic terms that are going to be used at trial but, nevertheless, it was understood that it was an approval by the United States for Croatia to launch Operation Storm. There were several conditions. Condition one, you are to minimise civilian casualties. Condition two, nothing is to happen to the UN forces, in Croatia. Condition three, you are to do it quickly and cleanly. The evidence will show that the Croatian government, after August 1st, prior to but also after August 1st, having received that approval, set out to ensure that the conditions given by the United States would be fulfilled. On the 2nd of August, the minister of defence calls a high-level meeting of all generals in other relevant military personnel. We have notes from that meeting. What did the defence minister tell all members of the military? "Military police must be energetic in its actions and must prevent all offences. "ZP or military district commanders must be the ones to pass on to the other commanders the prohibition of any kind of excessive conduct, (torching, looting, et cetera.) "We must not have a reason to put the heroes of the Homeland War on trial." And finally: "PB," which means the political affairs department of the Ministry of Defence, "workers must carry out their task of appropriately briefing HV members." And you will see later, Your Honours, that the political affairs department was the one that was charged with training in international humanitarian law, advising all units of their obligations under the Geneva Conventions and otherwise ensuring respect for the rule of both international and Croatian law. That same day at 17.30, the ministers of defence and the interior have a meeting to discuss security and how they are going to secure the area once military hostilities are over. Present at the meeting are Minister of Defence Susak, Minister of the Interior Jarnjak, Assistant Minister of the Interior Josko Moric, and the head of the military police, Mr. Mata [phoen] Lausic, whose name is not listed here because he is the author of these notes. Minister Jarnjak in point three says: "All MUP reserve units are to be mobilised on the 3rd and 4th of August, 1995, and they enter the liberated territories and take over power. "The police administration will be in Knin and Glina." That same day the head of the military police, Mr. Lausic, issues an order to ensure the implementation of the orders of the minister of defence and the minister of the interior, and he sends out his personal emissary from his office in Zagreb, a man named Major Juric, to be an intermediary to ensure that General Lausic's orders having been received from the minister of defence are implemented in the Split Military District. And he gives Major Juric the authority to replace military police commanders who are not effective in implementing the orders of the minister of defence ability interior and it says: "Major Juric in the command system he is superior to the 72nd Military Police Battalion and 73rd Military Police Battalion commanders." And below that: "He is responsible for the implementation of all military police tasks, in the 72nd Military Police zone of responsibility." It should be noted Mr. Juric and Mr. Lausic are not in General Gotovina's chain of command. They cannot issue orders to General Gotovina, nor can General Gotovina issue orders to them. On the 3rd of August the Assistant Minister of the Interior Mr. Moric and Mr. Lausic, the head of the military police, have a coordination meeting to draw up the plans that had been ordered by their respective ministers. General Lausic issues an order, says: "On 3 August 1995, a working meeting was held with representatives of the Ministry of the Interior at which the tactics and method of conduct of the military police and civilian police at the start of offensive operations in newly liberated areas of the Republic of Croatia were discussed. "In keeping with the conclusions and in order to ensure that they are implemented on all levels of command of units of the military police of the armed forces of the Republic of Croatia, I hereby order" and then the details are spelled out in the order. There is no question that the military police and the civilian police came up with a plan to prevent crime on the orders of the Croatian leadership and that those orders were implemented by Mr. Lausic on the military side and Mr. Moric on the civilian side. General Gotovina was not invited to these meetings. He was not asked to send a liaison officer to discuss the plans or how they would be implemented. In order to believe the Prosecution's case, you would have to conclude that a plan for security was drawn up prior to Operation Storm. It was ordered by the ministers of the interior and defence, given to the head of the military police and the assistant minister of the interior to work out the details. And then according to the Prosecution, Mr. Lausic turned around and subordinated the military police to General Gotovina, who is in nobody's chain of command and who is not present at any of the meetings. It is contrary to military logic. It is contradictory to common logic. It violates the principle of Occam's Razor. The Gotovina Defence submits to you, Your Honours, that the simple, straightforward explanation of the evidence is that plans were drawn up, given to Mr. Lausic and Mr. Moric. Mr. Lausic issued the orders, and Mr. Lausic throughout this time period remained in command of the implementation of these security plans. There will be no other interpretation of what happened. What did General Gotovina do as part of the planning to prevent crime? Part of the attack order for Operation Storm in the Split Military District, point 5: He orders the political affairs department to "Familiarising members with conduct in occupied settlements and handling of war booty. "Familiarising units with the need to eliminate all negative occurrences that will surface in the course of combat operations with a focus on preventing torching and destruction of larger populated areas and towns." 8: "Advising members of units on conduct with civilians and POWs in accordance with the Geneva Conventions." Part of what we believe is relevant is also what we discussed before, that General Gotovina set up his own officer training centre where international humanitarian law was taught. He called in Catholic bishops to try to teach his officers proper conduct in war. It should be kept in mind, the meeting of the 2nd of August and the exhortations of the minister of defence to prevent all unlawful conduct. At this point, Your Honour, the evidence is clear. All key institutions in the Republic of Croatia are attempting to prevent crime. The MUP, which is the ministry of the interior. The military police, you've seen the order to prevent crime from happening. The minister of defence, and military commanders including General Gotovina are all issuing orders to prevent crime. Occam's Razor. The Prosecution wants you to believe that a state and its ministers and its generals are issuing orders that they don't want followed. The Defence submits that the simple, straightforward answer is that ministers and commanders issue orders, and when they issue them they want them followed. Yet the Prosecution will have you believe that there was a joint criminal enterprise to allow crime to take place. To believe that, you have to believe that these orders were issued so as not to be followed. I also note in the operational diary the oral exhortations of the Split Military District command. "Knin must not experience the same treatment as Grahovo." Let's talk about the execution of Operation Storm. In the Vance Plan, which was the plan under which the United Nations peacekeepers came into Croatia, there is a point at paragraph 4 on page 448 on your screens. It says, the peacekeepers: "They would be required to be completely impartial between the various parties to the conflict." Your Honours, you will probably be surprised by the evidence in this trial, and the fact is the UN personnel did not maintain the neutrality that they were obligated to maintain under the Vance Plan. UN personnel -- as I had stated to you before, one of the US conditions allowing Operation Storm to proceed was that nothing could happen to UN personnel in Croatia. As a result, the Croatian government advised the United Nations on the evening of the 3rd of August that the operation would commence at 5.00 a.m. and that they were to take all necessary precautions to ensure the safety of UN personnel. So what did the personnel and the command in Sector South and Knin do? They violated their UN neutrality and immediately notified the Krajina Serb Main Staff in order to allow them to be ready for the attack and thus, from a military sense, taking away the element of surprise, which is one of the basic tenets of planning a military operation. How do we know this? We have two Krajina Serb military officers who have already provided evidence that this is what happened.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] At 4.14 I received a phone call from a liaison officer from headquarters, who was our government's liaison officer for UNPROFOR, to the effect that he had received information from an operational organ with UNPROFOR from Sector South command that the Croats would be attacking us. We were informed 18 times by various officers, French and such, informing us that we would be attacked in the morning at 5.00." General Sekulic there at the end refers to a French officer. He really means a French-Canadian officer in Knin and we will discuss that at trial as well, Your Honour. You will also see some evidence consistent with the evidence given by the Prosecution -- one of the Prosecution's star witnesses in the Milosevic case. He was a member of the Serbian intelligence services working with Belgrade in the so-called RSK. Here is what he has testified already to for the Prosecution, speaking now on behalf the Serb intelligence services: "Our sole objective was to obstruct the work of the ECMM, and later of the UN. We did everything to keep them from finding out the truth, and we repeatedly supplied them with misinformation. It was amazing to us how often they believed what we were saying. But if you keep repeating the same lies again and again, it seems as if anyone would eventually conclude that it must be true, that no one could lie so often and so consistently. "We also worked very hard to gain the trust of internationals and to have them come around to our point of view. We would do what we could to establish a rapport with them and then it made it much easier to have them accept our lies. No one would want to believe that their good friend would lie to them, so it made sense to use this approach, which I think we were more effective with than were the Croats." Second part of the statement which will become relevant as you have some of the witnesses start to appear, Your Honours. "The Serb secret services have continued these practices until today and they still control almost all, if not all, interpreters working for international agencies in Serb-held areas. It was encouraged that interpreters try to gain the trust of their principals so that their employer would want to take them with them to other assignments. "From early 1992 onwards, I was instructed by Zimonja to recruit UN and ECMM international personnel as cooperating agents of the RSK."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, you used the expression "star witness," which is in legal terms unknown to me. May I take it that you wanted to refer to an important or a prominent witness for the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let's use the word "insider witness" then, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That seems legally more commonly known, that expression.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, excuse me, and I'm sorry to interrupt my colleague but if we could move into private session for just one moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Please proceed, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, the evidence will show that the UN personnel in Knin were far from neutral and had become too close to the local Serb government and population. Indeed, they became so close that we will present evidence to you that dozens of UN personnel wound up marrying local Serbs and their translators. Let's discuss the planning of the use of artillery. Operation Storm was conducted in accordance with the US [Realtime transcript read in error "UN"] military doctrine known as AirLand battle. AirLand battle, one of the key tenets of air land battle is the so-called deep battle. Deep battle is the use of, amongst other things, artillery at the onset of an operation to achieve various purposes. From the US army field manual under "Pursuit, point 1: Artillery is used to "maintain pressure to demoralise the enemy with massed fires." Furthermore the Prosecution has submitted an expert report in this case which is a public document by Mr. Theunens. In Mr. Theunens's report here is what he writes about the purposes of artillery are. They are not simply, as the Prosecution yesterday left the impression, that it is exclusively to destroy military buildings. "Deep operations," according to the operations expert, "are directed against the enemy forces and functions beyond the close battle. Deep operations are executed at all levels with fires, manoeuvre, and leadership and expand the battlefield in space and time. The deep battle is designed to nullify the enemy's firepower, disrupt his command and control systems; destroy his supplies; and break his morale." When we were going through the Brioni transcripts, Your Honour, I said that President Tudjman used the word "demoralise." President Tudjman, as a military man, used the exact word that appears in the US army field manual and in the Prosecution's own expert report about what the legitimate purposes of artillery are. The suggestion that General Gotovina ordered shelling in order to put pressure on Serbs to leave is absurd. No military expert would question General Gotovina's decision to use artillery in support of his offensive operations. This is standard military practice, particularly under air land battle doctrine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, just for the correctness of the transcript, page 60, line 12, we find at this moment in the transcript that is UN military -- let me just check that for one second. UN military doctrine which I think you said US military.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: US military doctrine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: In terms of the planning, Your Honour, you noticed or should have noticed yesterday silence on fundamental issues like what targets did the Croatian army actually select in planning its artillery operation? What targets did the Croatian army actually select in planning its military operations? What targets did the Croatian army actually hit in executing its military operation? There was, to use an expression, radio silence from the Prosecution yesterday on these two fundamental issues. There were general references to proportionality, distinction, but with no reference to any evidence, any facts. We will submit those facts to you, Your Honours. The targets that were selected were exclusively military targets in Knin, Obrovac, Benkovac, Gracac, and Drnis. We know this. We have the documents for every town, and we will submit them to the Trial Chamber. The Prosecution wants you to believe that the Croats shelled civilian areas but offer you no evidence, nor has any been disclosed in discovery in this case, about what areas were targeted and what areas were hit. You don't have to just rely on our interpretations, Your Honours. There was no excessive shelling. There were such claims on the 4th of August, and as a result of the claims of people like UN personnel in Knin upon whom the Prosecution relies, the United Nations military observers conducted an investigation three weeks after the fact to determine whether these allegations were true. The findings were, at point 2: "In general shelling was concentrated against military objectives. The damages caused by shelling to civilian establishments is concentrated to the close vicinity of military objectives. Only few ... impacts," three to five, "is observed in other urban areas." This report, you will have to wait for the Defence case to get it, because this witness, the head of the UNMO, was on the Prosecution's witness list until the 1st of February. They pulled him. Why did they pull him? You will hear evidence from the Prosecution that Mr. Hjertnes the head of the UNMOs in Sector South, those findings by his team were subsequently overturned, overruled, different findings despite the fact that Mr. Hjertnes told the Prosecution in the middle of January that he has no idea what they are talking. The findings here say provisional, he testified under oath that a week later the final findings were submitted in the UN system and that they did not change. So the Prosecution removed him from their witness list in favour of two witnesses who are much lower-level subordinates of Mr. Hjertnes who will tell you that these findings were overturned. Here's the problem, Your Honours, and again I use the concept of Occam's Razor: There is no report that has been produced indicating that these findings were overturned. We have searched the entire UN system. There is no reference in any UN document to a finding subsequent to this report that there was excessive shelling or shelling of civilian areas. We have done a LexisNexis --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask you one thing in this respect. You said we will have to wait to see this report for the Defence case. Well, first of all, I don't know whether there will be any Defence case presented, so therefore that sounds a bit premature to me. At the same time, of course, I was not educated in the adversarial system, but putting such a report in cross-examination to the witness which apparently, although there's still litigation about that, apparently should replace the other witness, is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Sorry. We'd be happy to do it in cross-examination, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You tell us that we have to wait until the Defence case where I did not understand, from a procedural point of view, understand what the necessity of waiting was. And even if you wouldn't have such material, you know that the Chamber, and of course every party could take any initiative in that respect, could order a party to present evidence. I mean, that's within the power of the Chamber. So I thought you might be a bit over pessimistic about the procedural perspectives the Defence may have.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm very happy to hear that, Your Honour, and we'd be happy to submit that to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: As I said we've done a search of LexisNexis, Your Honours, to find any article ever written in the English language which references a subsequent report that the Croatian army shelled civilians or civilian areas and that this was a finding of the UNMOs and you find nothing. So to believe the Prosecution's theory, again Occam's Razor, the simple, straightforward answer is there's a report. It was filed. The author of the report says it wasn't changed. Therefore, that's the finding. To believe the Prosecution's case, this finding was overturned. There's no report, and there must have been some conspiracy because I would think that a finding that the Croatian army excessively shelled civilians would have been referenced by someone somewhere in the UN system or in the international media. We will leave it to you, Your Honours, to judge the credibility of the Prosecution's claims. In addition to this report as a result of the allegations that had been made on the 4th of August, the international media descended on Knin on the 7th of August expecting to find, to use two towns referenced by Mr. Tieger yesterday, Stalingrad or Vukovar. What did they find? Here is what Roy Gutman wrote of his findings, not just his findings, these were all international reporters were part of a pool. On the 7th of August: "At the United Nations base in Knin, UN officers chaffed at a continued curfew and restrictions on movements, but they acknowledged that the UN had overstated the damage to Knin during the height of fighting. "The UN commander, Brigadier-General Alain Forand of Canada had said that there had been no direct hits on Knin's hospital. Reporters saw ... large craters from shells that shattered most of the windows in a nearby apartment house but there was no evidence of indiscriminate shelling." United States Ambassador Galbraith will testify before you. He will tell you that military attaches of foreign countries including the United States also went to Knin on the 7th of August to investigate the claims of excessive shelling. And he will tell you that there was no excessive shelling and that was the finding of his military attache as well as military attaches of several other countries. One Prosecution witness will tell you, Mr. Tieger pointed out and left the impression that the Croatian army had hit the Knin hospital. Here's what really happened according to the Prosecution's own witness. He's talking about a visit to Knin on the 7th with Mr. Akashi and he says: "I remember that the one question that had come up is whether the Knin hospital had been targeted by fire, by either side, and we did speak with a nurse who indicated that, at one point early in the fighting, I believe it would have been on the 5th of August or perhaps the 4th, an RSK tank had been positioned very close to the hospital and had been sending outgoing fire and had also been targeted apparently by Croatian army units. In fact, there was almost no evidence of damage to the hospital that we could see. There was one sign of an impact that we were shown, but it caused minor structural damage to the building. So this contradicted early reports we had heard that the hospital had sustained major damage. That did not appear to be the case." Your Honours, there's going to be a lot of discussion about the Brioni transcript in this case. We believe we have the right interpretation of it. The Prosecution will believe that they have the right interpretation of it. The question is: What is the best way for you to decide who has the better of the argument? We submit, Your Honours, that the best way is to look to see what did the subordinates of President Tudjman do? How did they act after the Brioni meeting? Did they implement a plan to target civilians, civilian buildings? Did they implement a plan which hit civilian targets and civilian buildings, or did they target exclusively military targets, as we have -- as we will show according to the documents, and did they only hit military targets as indicated by the various pieces of evidence that I have now alerted you to? We submit, Your Honours, that you should interpret the Brioni transcript in accordance with how the Croatian commanders themselves would have interpreted the words that President Tudjman was saying. After all, that is the only relevant issue with respect to that transcript. What I think about it, what Mr. Tieger thinks about it, how the Trial Chamber itself may have interpreted those words is really somewhat irrelevant. The question is how did the subordinates interpret those words, and we believe you should look to the evidence. The evidence shows the Croatian commanders, specifically my client, Ante Gotovina, did not interpret anything that President Tudjman said as being an order to excessively shell civilians or civilian targets. How did we get these false claims of excessive shelling? Where does this come from, you may ask yourselves. We can explain that to you as well, Your Honours. False claims of excessive shelling were put forward as propaganda by the Krajina Serbs themselves at 6.30 in the morning on the 4th. This is a report, a protest sent by General Mrksic to General Forand in the UNPROFOR command in Zagreb, at 6.30 -- sorry, to General Janvier. I apologise. "Long range artillery fire began at exactly 0500 hours this morning on 4 August against all civilian targets in the towns of Knin, Benkovac, Obrovac, Drnis, Vrgin Most, Vojnic, Glina, Petrinja, and most populated places in the western part of Krajina and in the areas of Eastern Slavonia, Western Srem, and Baranja. Simultaneously with this protest note Mrksic's liaison officer, Colonel Novakovic, called General Janvier. We have a record of what General Janvier was told by Kosta Novakovic at 6.30 in the morning on the 4th. He alerts General Janvier to the fact that the protest note has come and he said at third paragraph: "This morning at 0500, HV and HVO forces conducted general aggression, targeting civilian objects in all inhabited areas of the RSK especially in Knin on which thousands of shells fell. "They have destroyed numerous buildings; there are casualties amongst the civilian population including women, children and the elderly. "They targeted the immediate vicinity of UNPROFOR Sector South command using direct fire. "They also targeted the hospital and other similar buildings, firing randomly and without any order; UNPROFOR officers located there can confirm these claims." As we know, Your Honour, claims such as the Croats targeting the hospital were false. This was propaganda that had been put out and in fact passed along by the UN Sector South command. It is important to note that the UN commanders in Knin on the 4th of August never went out in the town to examine whether the claims of General Mrksic and Colonel Novakovic were actually true. Nevertheless, they sent that report relying on Mrksic and Novakovic, and I refer you back to Mr. Lazarevic's testimony about how easy it had become to lie and lie and to have the UNCRO commanders believe it. And they lied again and the UNCRO commanders believed it again and they sent it up the chain of command. They sent it up so far that by 2.00 p.m. on the 4th of August Carl Bildt, the chair -- one of the co-chairmen and the representative of the European Union issued the following statement at paragraph three, sentence three -- sorry, sentence two: "Especially appalling is the shelling of the civilian population now being reported. It should be remembered that Krajina Serb president Mr. Martic had been indicted for war crimes following the Serb rocket attack in Zagreb in May. It is difficult to see any difference between these actions and the shelling of Knin which President Tudjman must now be held responsible for." This is 2.00 on the 4th of August and no one from the UN had gone out to actually investigate whether this was true. This was a rush to judgement. And as a result of statements like this from Mr. Bildt, the international press descended on Knin, as I said earlier, found the conclusions to be inaccurate, and as a result of statements like this the UNMOs conducted their own investigation and concluded that the allegations were false. But as Mr. Lazarevic, the insider witness in Milosevic, said, they had come under the influence, the UNCRO command in Knin had come under the influence of Serb officers, and that will be proven by the evidence at trial. Your Honours, another comment. The evidence of these Canadian officers upon whom the Prosecution's indiscriminate shelling case relies has been in their possession since 1995 and 1996. There is nothing new in this case over the last 13 years with respect to those allegations. Yet I call your attention to the amended indictment in this case, confirmed in February of 2004 and ask you to search that document and see if you can find the words "shelling" or "artillery" or any variation of those words in the amended indictment in this case. If the evidence is so strong, beyond reasonable doubt, that the testimony of these UNCRO commanders in Knin is that strong and has been in their possession for 12 or 13 years now, why is it that the words "artillery" or "shelling" appear only in the 2006 as part of a new allegation against General Gotovina alleging him to be a member of a joint criminal enterprise. The answer you will find at the conclusion of the Prosecution's case. They need some intentional act, some bad act by Ante Gotovina to justify why he's even here. You didn't see an illegal order issued by General Gotovina yesterday. They acknowledged that he has issued repeated orders for conduct, maintaining the rule of law. If the shelling issue is not here, what is the bad act that General Gotovina committed? We submit to you there is no other bad act. There is no other way to get him into a joint criminal enterprise unless you want to now believe that the excessive shelling case which wasn't worthy of being mentioned in the amended indictment suddenly is the linchpin of the Prosecution's case and not a single piece of relevant evidence has changed in 13 years. Your Honours, this might be an opportunity for a break if you wish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. May I inquire how much time you or Mr. Kehoe would need after this break?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: We're going to go to the end, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You'll go to the very end.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we will have a break. We will resume at 25 minutes to 1.00 and then you've got one hour and 10 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before I give you the opportunity to continue, Mr. Misetic, there still seems to be a problem about the operative indictment. The indictment that was filed on the 22nd of February had as its title, and that was a remainder from the past, "Proposed amended indictment." So we ordered the Prosecution -- or invited the Prosecution to refile it but now without the word "proposed" because it was the operative indictment. To my understanding this has not been done yet which creates confusion as to what the operative indictment is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And that -- I had hoped it would have been completed before we were -- there was some problem with the presence of the Prosecutor to sign it and make it official but it's definitely on our radar screen and the operative documents have been prepared.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then the Chamber expects the Prosecution to deal with that without further delay. At the same time, I now put it on the record that since the only thing the Chamber expects that will change is to take out the word "proposed," that the content of the indictment as filed on the 22nd of February is the operative indictment. Mr. Misetic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, do I want to correct the record. Mr. Tieger alerted me to the fact that in fact the Steinar Hjertnes UNMO report is a 92 ter exhibit with one of their witnesses. So I did want that -- to clarify that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You mean we don't have to wait --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That's correct. Just to correct the record, Your Honour, and I regret the error.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, why did the Krajina Serbs leave on the 4th of August? Because they -- the leadership of the Krajina Serbs had a plan to evacuate its civilians. They trained and had exercises to be ready to implement that plan, and on the 4th of August they implemented it. On the 4th of August -- let me take a step back. You will hear evidence, Your Honours, that from UN personnel they had reported at 1500 on the 4th of August that the situation in Knin was now calm, that people were exiting their homes after the initial shelling in the morning and were cleaning up the broken glass, at 1500 on the 4th. At 16.45, Milan Martic, and it's on your screens, issues the evacuation order to evacuate the civilian population. Point 1 states: "To begin the planned evacuation of all inhabitants unfit for combat from the following municipalities," and lists them. Point 2 says: "To evacuate them the evacuation shall be carried out in a planned manner according to the existing planned directions towards Knin and then through Otric towards Srb and Lapac." The Prosecution yesterday suggested to the Trial Chamber that this order was not intended to evacuate the civilians permanently out of the so-called Krajina but that the plans were only to evacuate them internally to Srb and Lapac, which are towns in Croatia. We submit to you, Your Honours, that that is not an interpretation supported by the evidence. It is true that Martic's order says to go to Srb and Lapac, but that is because the existing plans that had already been prepared said that. In reality, the order that was issued said to go to Bosanski Petrovac in Bosnia and to Banja Luka in Bosnia. How do we know this? At 19.53 on the evening of the 4th, the UN reported the following at paragraph 4 of this document: "We have been advised by the civil affairs office in Sector South that the Knin leadership have requested UNHCR and UNPF assistance in evacuating approximately 32.000 civilians from Benkovac, Obrovac, Gracac, and Knin to Petrovac and Banja Luka in Bosnia and Herzegovina." We have more than this. We have the Krajina Serb leaders themselves on video for you to see describing the atmosphere around Milan Martic and General Mrksic on the afternoon of the 4th and how it was that the decision to evacuate the entire civilian population from so-called Krajina to Bosnia was taken. We'd like to play that video for you now. The speaker is the mayor of Knin, Drago Kovacevic who was a high-ranking member of Martic's inner circle at the time and who was present when these conversations and the decision was taken to evacuate the civilian population.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] Martic was in uniform. There was a huge ashtray in front of him, several empty packs of cigarettes, and we exchanged greetings. Why had he called me? He called me because he said, I've decided to evacuate the city and we should take steps to relocate the civilian population. And I must stress this, civilian population from Northern Dalmatia, meaning the municipalities of Benkovac, Obrovac, Knin, Drnis, and the municipality of Gracac in Lika. "This does did not come to as a shock to me. I perceived this to be some sort of a rational measure. At that moment, we passed the order. Kosta Novakovic specifically passed the order. "It was then that we wrote in the order that this was to evacuate the civilian population, meaning in the direction of Knin, Otric, Srb, or Lapac, which were the areas where the people were to be relocated to. It was then that Mrksic reacted and said, What do you mean by Srb? We need to go further than Srb, he says. Further towards Petrovac and Banja Luka. And then he expressed a reservation. He said if the civilians started leaving, the military lines would be facing a problem. He says if the civilians go, the army will go after them to evacuate them and we are going to have enormous problems. "However, sometime that evening when he arrived, Mrksic was somewhere on the floor above, he told me on the stairs that the evacuation of the population had been ordered. I told him, "General, the army will fall apart. What do you mean by evacuating the people and doing this by means of an order?" He says this is not in our hands. It was the Supreme Defence Council that took that decision. "And then someone requested that Martic -- it was Martic himself who requested to be put through to Slobo, to spoke to Slobo and he spoke not to Slobo but to Brane Crncevic. So he got hold of Brane Crncevic who assured him that he probably couldn't get hold of Slobo, which was why he spoke to Brane, and then he was told by him, No, no, he won't take any steps. Slobo wouldn't do anything in this case. And then for the first time I heard Martic cursing Slobo and so on and so forth."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, the evidence in this case is going to be overwhelmingly clear that the Krajina Serb leadership under Milan Martic, as they had in Western Slavonia, as they had prepared to do for the 90 days prior to Operation Storm, evacuated their own population rather than allow them to live in a multi-ethnic state. It was part and parcel of the ideology that reigned in the so-called Krajina. As referenced in the Prosecution's pre-trial brief in Martic, the ideology was: There can be no co-existence with Croats. The Serbs can only feel safe in a homogeneous, ethnically-Serb state. That was the mentality that had been imposed by the Greater Serbian ideology of the time. We know this from a video from the 7th of August, discussing now in retrospect what had just occurred. This is real evidence taken in realtime on the 7th of August, 1995. It involves a man named Savo Strbac. This is a name you will hear repeatedly and extensively throughout this trial. Mr. Strbac is a key member of Martic's joint criminal enterprise who was among the leadership of the Krajina Serbs, who was ideologically committed to the ideology of an ethnically pure Greater Serbia. He made these statements to the international media repeatedly in the years prior to Operation Storm. He repeatedly stated that Serbs will only accept a unified Greater Serbia and that no co-existence with Croats was possible. After Operation Storm, Mr. Strbac formed his own "humanitarian centre" and became an associate of the Office of the Prosecutor in assisting the Prosecutor's office in obtaining witnesses for this case. Mr. Strbac even received a letter of recommendation from the Prosecution to assist him in raising money for his efforts. The following video was taken on the 7th of August, 1995. It is Mr. Strbac explaining from a TV studio in Banja Luka to the Serb population why the decision had been taken to take the civilians out of the so-called Krajina. In this video you will see the very mind-set of which I speak, the mind-set of the ideology of an ethnically pure Greater Serbia.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] The Croats never intended to live with the Serbs in the former Croatia. "This was now most clearly demonstrated by the latest examples of their aggression in Western Slavonia and now in Dalmatia, Lika, Banija and Kordun. All of us who were in a position to speak to international players constantly kept warning them that -- about this fact and spoke about this, that the Croats didn't want to live with us and that we cannot allow ourselves to live with them so that the genocide committed against us in the past would not be repeated. And I use the term we must not allow ourselves because it has a stronger meaning than we do not wish to live with them simply. We do not and cannot of course live with them and because of this it was necessary first and foremost that we preserve our biological potential. Our people could have become extinct. The civilian population could have been killed. Our civilians and women could have been killed. We need our biological potential for something that is hopefully yet to come. "On the day of the most recent aggression against Krajina my association, the Veritas, wrote a letter to Boutros-Ghali alerting him about these things, a never before seen massacre which would be launched against the Serb population which is why it was decided in the end to begin the exodus in order to protect the people."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, the decision was taken to preserve our biological potential. That is the ideology at play here on the Krajina Serb side. That is the reason that leaders of the Krajina Serbs and indeed leaders of the Milosevic JCE from Western Slavonia to Sarajevo to Kosovo evacuate their civilians, to preserve their biological potential. I turn next to the issue of crime prevention. You've already seen the orders of General Gotovina and the attack order for Operation Storm concerning the implementation of international humanitarian law and the prevention of looting. You've seen the Split Military District diary entry saying Knin must not suffer the same fate as Grahovo. We now have for you the entry in the operational diary on the morning of the 5th of August as General Gotovina's forces, as he is advised that his forces are about to enter Knin. General Gotovina issues the order orally: "He ordered maximum fairness in treatment of civilians and behaviour towards the UN. This order has been passed to all operative groups and commanders." General Gotovina in the execution of the operation is issuing orders for maximum correctness to civilians and the UN. Nevertheless, it is true that when the troops entered Knin, in their state of jubilation they began to engage looting. Not of any great scale, and that will be confirmed for you by the United Nations itself, sitreps of the United Nations, as well as a video that we will show you at trial of the UN on the 7th saying, Croatian troops in Knin are behaving "professionally and correctly." Why, on the 7th, are they behaving professionally and correctly? The Prosecution referenced a video of what General Gotovina did when he entered Knin on the 6th. It is important for you to keep in mind that General Gotovina conducted Operation Storm from his headquarters in Bosnia. It is important to keep in mind and this is what Mr. Kehoe was referring to in his portion, that the objectives of the Croatian army were centered in Bosnia. And Operation Storm for General Gotovina was simply a left turn to take one portion of territory and to come back to his headquarters in Bosnia and be prepared for further operations in Bosnia where he had been since the winter of 1994. Again, I repeat that General Gotovina was in Bosnia from the winter of 1994. General Gotovina came into Knin on the morning of the 6th after having issued written orders, after having issued oral orders, seeing troops breaking glass, drinking, and otherwise in a state of exultation and videotaped a meeting with his commanders, all of whom thought that General Gotovina was about to praise them for winning the war and taking the capital of the Krajina Serbs. This is General Gotovina in realtime on the 6th. It is my suggestion but obviously it's up to the Trial Chamber, I think it's important that the Trial Chamber hears General Gotovina's voice during this. It's a six-minute video, but obviously I'll leave it to the Trial Chamber, I've been told by the booths that if it's changed to B/C/S you can read along with the subtitles. If you prefer the translations, we'll have to replay it again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think the Chamber has the choice to hear the original on channel 6. If you could assist us in telling us approximately when we should move to what approximately the language that immediately precedes the moment --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I will stop it and tell you to change it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll move to 6 and then we'll read the English and then we'll hear what you'd like to us to hear. Then please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] And all the rest that was tasked, the tasks that were issued last night and I'm now calling upon you to account for yourselves. Security services, Generalic, did he pass it on to Loza? First, did the political affairs department do its job? No, it didn't. Ceko, you were at the meeting, weren't you? Zelic was here; he had other tasks. You were at the meeting. What have you done since last night? Was the County Prefect contacted? Did you verify whether the County Prefect was contacted? Was civilian protection requested? Were the firefighters requested? They have been requested, General. And where are they then? Do you realise that everything has to be ready by 5.00 this afternoon, everything? Was it that difficult to find just a single cross here? A single cross. Skoric, where's the cross? "We couldn't find one, it should be coming -- "You didn't find a cross, you fucking imbecile. Had you stopped in Sinj by the church there and asked the friar there to give you a cross, he'd have given you ten of those. Because you are idiots, incompetent. But you're good enough to pose in front of those cameras, those screens to be photographed. You're good enough to do that. Just one example, you weren't even able to get hold of a single cross."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I think now might be an appropriate time.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] Let me not even begin to mention what I could see in the town. It's a disgrace. A disgrace. Barbarians and vandals act like that, those who are paid with war booty and wage war for war booty. "The unit commanders from Sinj to Knin, with the help of the engineers, have the task today to get the entire road in order. Everything, the vehicles, all that dirt, throw it out. Clean it up. Clear it. The army is not to be seen in the streets. The military police is not in groups but is deployed at all check-points. They took a map of the town as planned and systematically set up check-points and assumed control of the town. The military police commanders are patrolling. Patrol vehicles are patrolling the town. Cooperation with the civilian authorities in the form of the civilian police is to be established until General Cermak, who has just arrived this morning, can take over these matters and take matters into his own hands. And until then, if he's left alone, by 5.00 tonight nothing will be ready but we'll have chaos again. What a disgrace. Do you realise the prime minister is coming, the ministers, the minister of transportation and all that. Everybody arriving today will enter into a town that the Croatian army went through and which it still had under its control because the civilian authorities haven't taken over yet. Who are you trying to embarrass? You are embarrassing yourselves and those under your command for whom you are responsible. And all of our people who died, who were killed, you are responsible, people who gave their lives for this, you should have a little respect because people have died for the sake of Knin and all the way from Dinara since this winter, last October. Not to mention the recent operations and how many perished and how many are still in hospital to this very day and those maimed for life. And yet you behave like this and you call yourselves commanders. Security. What is security? Security must be organised. It's in control of the situation. The military police must obey. They are the executors, the technical executors. They are the guardians of the code of honour of the armed forces. It guarantees the implementation and application of all of that in the field. "Political affairs department. I don't see any posters in the street. No flags at any of the major facilities, installations. Nothing. Where is -- where is all of that? "Being put up as we speak, General? "What's being put up? Where is it? It's 11.30. Since this morning, since 4.00 in fact, you should have been doing this all through the night. A helicopter is available. Everything is available to pursue this with total efficiency and yet you don't know how to make use of all of this. If you don't know how to work, do your job, something, whatever. Since nobody dragged you by your hair to become what you are, then gentlemen, go ahead and join the infantry, go into battle. You'll end up saying well, I was -- I am a warrior. The fuck you are. Every day is a new day for a warrior and every day a warrior has to prove himself over and over again."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution described those orders from General Gotovina yesterday as boilerplate and routine. I suggest to you, Your Honours, that if one of us were yelled at by our superiors like that we would not consider that to be boilerplate or routine. What happened on the 6th of August? It is a critical day. The Prosecution presented a map yesterday which I believe is misleading to the Trial Chamber in that it suggests it was a map of General Gotovina's forces and the days where they were stationed as Operation Storm progressed and the overlay, and this is the map, the overlay then is -- these are -- these are General Gotovina's forces advancing in the period of 4 August through the 8th or 9th of August, but the killings, wanton destruction, plunder, are for the period through the 30th of September, 1995. We believe that's misleading to the Trial Chamber, Your Honours, because on the 6th of August the civilian government of the Republic of Croatia consistent with the plans that had been drawn up and ordered by Ministers Susak and Jarnjak, took control of territories as the Croatian army was advancing on the front line. What that means as a matter of law is that these territories immediately returned to the constitutional order of the Republic of Croatia and the civilian government had jurisdiction over these lands. I'd like to show you now a video of the 6th of August of the minister of the interior establishing the police station in Knin and appointing an ethnic Serb as the head of the Croatian police administration in Knin.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] Dear Mr. Chief, please allow me to hand over to you the signboard bearing the inscription Republic of Croatia Ministry of the Interior police administration Knin. It is provided by the constitutional law on ethnic minorities of the Republic of Croatia that Knin has a district and, accordingly, the police administration should now be established in Knin. Since, according to the aforementioned law, an Assembly has not been established and upon this Assembly's proposal the chief shall be appointed by the government of the Republic of Croatia, I hereby appoint you acting chief until an election takes place whereupon the Assembly will nominate to the government of the Republic of Croatia a chief. Until such time, I am assigning you this duty provided by the constitution of the Republic of Croatia and the laws of the Republic of Croatia. Your task shall be to establish the civilian authorities in Knin and in the area of your police administration. In your own area of responsibility, you are to link up with the police administration of Zadar. Congratulations to you."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: On the 6th of August, General Gotovina turned over control of the town of Knin to the civilian government and General Gotovina left to continue offensive operations in Operation Storm to the north of Knin. It is important to note that as the Croatian army took territory, it immediately turned over jurisdiction of that territory to the civilian government. I think the best way for the Trial Chamber to hear this is to hear it from the minister of the interior himself who held a press conference on the 8th of August and went and explained in great detail the constitutional order of the Republic of Croatia, what the security plans were and who had jurisdiction over the territory referenced in the map that the Prosecution submitted yesterday. This is Minister of the Interior Jarnjak on the 8th of August.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] Good evening. This conference is now open. I would like to welcome the minister of the interior of the Republic of Croatia, Mr. Ivan Jarnjak. "Ladies and gentlemen, good evening. Please allow me to inform you about the current and future activities of the Ministry of the Interior throughout the areas that are now being liberated. The constitutional and legal order of the Republic of Croatia is now being introduced to the liberated areas. In order to accomplish this, it is necessary for the Ministry of the Interior, along with other institutions, to enter those areas with its forces. Following the Croatian army and the special units of the Ministry of the Interior, the civilian police entered those areas as well, immediately after them establishing basic police and border police stations. "Following state policy guidelines, already in 1992 the Ministry of the Interior developed the organisational structure of two of these police administration and police stations for the entire Republic of Croatia including the territories that have now been liberated. Therefore, we've had the entire organisational structure in place since 1992. Now we are merely implementing it. "Of all the police stations that had been expelled from their respective areas during the aggression, those police stations that had been expelled in 1991 and 1992 in part they continued operating in such areas as they had been relocated to. Now they return to their own original areas, those being the police stations Lovinac, Drnis, Vrlika, Kijevo, Slunj, Petrinja, Glina, and Hrvatska Kostajnica. The expelled police substations have also been returned, those being Cetingrad, Saborsko, Plaski and Lasinje. "The border police have become operational in Hrvatska Kostajnica, Kijevo, Slunj, Donji Lapac, Strmica, Donji Srb and Licko Petrovo Selo. Police stations are prepared to receive the border police in Dvor and Topusko. "According to the constitutional law on human rights and liberties, the rights of ethnic communities and minorities, police administrations which must be organised according to these laws have become operational. Those being the Knin police administration and the Glina police administration. Those are districts according to this constitutional law which have special statutes. In those areas, of course, police stations have also been established for Knin, Donji Lapac, Gracac, Korenica, Benkovac, and Obrovac. Those are the police administrations which are part of -- or, rather, police stations which are part of this police administration. "For the district of Glina, the police administration has been established with the police stations Glina, Vojnic, and Hrvatska Kostajnica. The police stations of Vrgin Most and Dvor are ready to go back to their areas of operation. "Immediately after the Croatian army and the Special Police of the Ministry of the Interior completed the first part of their task and the combat operations and activities ceased, members of the Ministry of the Interior entered the populated localities and started securing the populated localities and the communications connecting those localities and controlling and directing the traffic. "At the same time as police stations and police substations were being established, all services of the Ministry of the Interior became operational, meaning civil protection, the firefighters, while pre-conditions are also being created for the establishment of services that conduct civil affairs, that is specifically issuing Croatian documents. The Civil Protection Units have started clearing the field in terms of removing small livestock and cattle, taking care of the abandoned movable property and any real estate left behind, first in the settled areas and then over the following days this will also be the case in non-populated areas. Probably over the next couple of days. "To all those residing in the newly liberated areas, to those who remained and to those who will return, hereby I mean displaced persons, we guarantee personal safety, safety for their property. We guarantee public law and order that we shall uphold. "Thank you very much. "Thank you, Minister Jarnjak."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, there was one more question and I believe it was raised in the Prosecutor's opening statement regarding this allegation that, yes, the Ministry of Interior and the constitutional order of the Republic of Croatia had been restored, but somehow the argument was advanced that everybody knew that they really couldn't do their jobs or they weren't prepared or they weren't ready, and then the issue was raised about jurisdiction over investigations of crimes committed by soldiers. This question was asked by a reporter of the Washington Post. It concerns an incident of the Bosnian army crossing from the Bihac pocket into Croatia and allegedly burning down Serb villages and the following question and answer were posed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: "Minister Washington Post Gene Rupert. [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] I have no information concerning this matter. However, when we come to that area and any area, the police will establish the actual state of affair, carry on-site investigations at each facility, take records and then establish whether it was caused by combat activities or something else. Then I will be able to give a specific answer to your question."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Furthermore, Your Honours, on the 8th of August, it's important to note that the justice system had been restored to the newly liberated areas. Courts had been put in place, civilian courts in Knin on the 8th of August and we have video of the president of the Supreme Court of Croatia and the Minister of Justice Mr. Separovic in Knin on the 8th of August establishing the civilian court system.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] The president of the Supreme Court of the Republic of Croatia Krunoslav Olujic and the Minister of Justice Miroslav Separovic visited Knin today. At the building of the Municipal court a work meeting was held with the presidents of the county courts in Sibenik, Split and Zadar. It has been concluded that the municipal court in Knin headed by Milovan Curko, should become operational as soon as possible. "The Minister of Justice, that is the competent county court, made a decision according to which the seat, that is the temporary seat of the municipal court in Knin is relocated from Sibenik to Knin. Today we opened the building in Knin and the fact that from this day the building of the municipal court in Knin is for practical purposes open means that a legal State of Croatia has become functional in those areas and that the implementation of the rule of law as one of the fundamental principles of the Croatian constitutional order has begun. "I am confident that this is a new beginning, a beginning where the municipal court in Knin will guarantee all human rights to all citizens who live here and contribute to the rule of the constitution and the laws of the Republic of Croatia. "The high level delegation continued its visit to the area in Drnis."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, again I want to -- I wish to reiterate the point why we went through that exercise is because the constitutional order of the Republic of Croatia and civilian institutions were back in the territory. This map would therefore lead you to believe because it -- because the crimes committed after Storm through the 30th of September are overlaid on a map of General Gotovina's conduct of battle for four days in early August, it would lead you to think that the Croatian army held this territory through the 30th of September or was otherwise responsible for security and that is not the case. The fact of the matter is Croatian troops were not in control of this territory after hostilities ended on the 9th of August. General Gotovina continued to nevertheless issue orders for compliance with discipline. He issued the following order on the 10th of August: "Based on the information from the areas liberated by the HV, the analysis thereof and in order to prevent theft of property, undisciplined conduct, and to save human lives I hereby order. "I prohibit arbitrary movement of the HV members of liberated areas without the knowledge of --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Kindly slow down for the interpreters, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Sorry. I'll go to point 2: "Take all necessary measures and fully engage in the implementation of the military disciplinary conduct and the maintenance of order in the areas of responsibility, and prevent arson and all other illegal acts. Take resolute measures against anybody to conducts himself in an undisciplined manner." When we talk about murders, the state of the evidence in this case is that there is not a single piece of evidence that would suggest that General Gotovina ever had any information about anybody being unlawfully killed. The Prosecution yesterday talked about subordination of General Gotovina's sanitation units and then reports were sent to somebody else but I didn't hear in that argument that a report was ever sent to General Gotovina informing him of anything improper in terms of unlawful killing. There would have been no reason for anyone to inform General Gotovina about this. That's why there are no reports. There is no reason, because the civilian government was in charge of the area. The civilian police had primary jurisdiction to investigate any murder committed by anyone, to document it, to get the civilian prosecutors on board, and to investigate it. There was no reason for anyone ever to let General Gotovina know of any unlawful killing, and it never happened. I again refer to Occam's principle. You will see in the evidence in this case, Your Honours, that despite the fact that there were indeed problems in coordination and implementation of the plans to provide security in the area, within the Croatian government itself nobody ever sent a message to General Gotovina that he had to take some measures. Nobody asked him to come to a meeting to say, We can't do our jobs. You need to do something. The international agencies and organisations in the region also did not seek meetings with General Gotovina to advise him of crimes being committed, because he was not a person who was responsible for security in the area. We will show you a videotape at trial of a meeting between General Gotovina and General Forand of Canada on the 8th of August and in that video you will see there was nothing but praise for General Gotovina, his conduct of hostilities, and the fact that when he turned the town of Knin over, he had restored order when he turned over the town to the civilian government. While we do not dispute that certain incidents did indeed occur of murder, the fact is that there are other incidents that will be contested in this case. There are situations, as the Trial Chamber is aware, where cause of death has not been determined, where a body has not been found, indeed, even to this day there are multiple names on the Prosecution's schedule of killings that turn out to be one and the same person. So we will go through that evidence in trial, Your Honours. We do ask you to keep in mind that the Prosecution must obviously prove that someone was a non-combatant. The evidence in this trial will show, again according to the Krajina Serb generals themselves, that the average age of the Krajina Serb soldier was 47 years old. Several companies of the RSK had an average age of 56 years old. If that is the average, it is likely at that there were people in their 60s who were active combatants. We therefore ask the Trial Chamber to keep this in mind and keep the Prosecution to its proof that a particular person was a non-combatant. It is important to note at this point, again why that introduction was important about the context of what was going on. General Gotovina was in Bosnia for a year, only had a slight detour to come back to Croatia to conduct Operation Storm. He had been fighting active combat from the 23rd of July in what was know as Operation Summer 95 all the way through the 10th of August in active combat, as were his front-line troops. On orders of his superiors, he was given leave on the 11th of August. He had recently gotten married and left and spent five days on islands off the coast of Croatia. This is relevant piece of evidence for us because ultimately you will have to conclude what were General Gotovina's responsibilities as told to him by his superiors. We submit to you, Your Honours, General Gotovina was an operational commander who had been tasked by his superiors to conduct offensive operations and keep himself focused on being prepared for the next phase of hostilities, which would soon happen. Indeed, they happened so soon that while General Gotovina was on leave on the 13th and 14th of August, General Mladic executed a counter-offensive against General Gotovina's forces in Bosnia, killing 28 members of the Croatian army. General Gotovina cut short his leave in order to retake command as a result of that counter-offensive. General Gotovina was preoccupied with events in Bosnia. That was the task that was given to him by his military commanders, and the area in his rear, which was now liberated territory in the constitutional order of the Republic of Croatia, had been left intentionally to other agencies of the Croatian government to act in accordance with the law and in accordance with their obligations under the constitution of the Republic of Croatia. We submit to the Trial Chamber that if anyone had perceived at the head of the State of Croatia that General Gotovina was responsible for security, he would not have been given leave of five days to just rest. Instead, that leave was intended for him to -- for him and his front-line forces, I would also add that his front-line forces were given leave at the same time, having been in active combat for 17 days. They were on leave. And indeed when General Gotovina came back on the 16th, the next day he was asked to come to Zagreb because a high-level US delegation led by Mr. Holbrooke and General Wesley Clark were in Zagreb to discuss future Croatian activities in Bosnia and General Gotovina was in Zagreb preparing the next phase of the hostilities, which were to defeat General Mladic on the battlefield. As you heard earlier, President Clinton had been convinced that only by defeating Mladic's forces could there be a negotiation that would ultimately leave -- lead to the Dayton Peace Agreement. General Gotovina was not perceived by anyone in the Croatian government or anyone in the international forces or organisations on the ground as being the person to go to to resolve security issues. Everyone understood, including the UNCRO commanders in Knin, that General Gotovina was in Bosnia and was tasked with different objectives. General Gotovina, Your Honours, was not Superman. He was and is a human being who could only do so much. He was entitled, as stated in the von Leeb case, to rely on those other institutions, to rely on commanders in his rear, to rely on the civilian government of the Republic of Croatia to take care of the security situation. He did his job. He defeated -- he fulfilled the objectives that had been laid out for him which was win the war. He did it all the time by issuing orders, energetically advising his troops of their obligations, instituting training programmes, inviting Catholic bishops, constantly trying to take this new army which didn't exist in 1991 and give it a professional level. And I submit to you, Your Honours, that in the three years that General Gotovina had a chance to do what he could, he did his job nobly. And I dare say that I do not know of other commanders who would have done a better job. There were indeed problems in restoring law and order to this region. We concede that point. The issue is what was the intent? The fundamental problem in this case from our perspective is that the Prosecution starts from the position, as will some of the Prosecution's witnesses, that crime happened, and because crime happened, and crime happened on a wide-scale level, the Trial Chamber is to assume or to draw the conclusion that this was "ordered from the top." Mr. Tieger repeated several times yesterday, this is criminal. Why can't something be done? What Mr. Tieger avoided discussing yesterday was any concrete proposal from the Prosecution, from any Prosecution witness, as to what it is they think could have been done to materially change the situation as it existed when Croatia took 10.500 square kilometres of territory and tried to impose the rule of law in a relatively short period of time. There is a reason why the Prosecution and its witnesses avoid that discussion, because the answer is not easy. The question must be asked: If it weren't Croatian forces or the Croatian government or the Croatian police, if this area had been taken over by the best fighting force in the world committed to international humanitarian law, NATO, if the civilian authority had been given to the defender of human rights in the world, the United Nations, would they have taken steps that would have simply solved the problem in a snap as implied by the Prosecution? We don't have to guess on the answer to that question. We will repeatedly ask the Prosecution's witnesses to speak concretely about what steps were so obvious that could have been taken that weren't, that the failure to take those steps would amount to recklessness or wilful indifference to the crime being committed in this area. We will ask witnesses to compare the situation, particularly the international witnesses, who were also later involved in events in Kosovo in 1999. We want to discuss the situation there because we believe it is important for the Trial Chamber to have some frame of reference when we review these facts. How did NATO and the UN fare when they had the legal obligations in Kosovo after June of 1999 to protect civilians, protect their property, and maintain the rule of law and law and order? You will find the statistics show that similar to what happened in Croatia, the same problems were encountered by NATO and the UN in Kosovo. In the six months after the international community took control of Kosovo, according to Human Rights Watch, 1000 Serbian civilians were killed, tens of thousands of Serbian homes were destroyed, uncountable property was looted, 76 Orthodox churches were destroyed or partially destroyed. The question must be raised: If it is so simple to restore order to 10.500 square kilometres of territory, and I note that both Kosovo and the so-called Krajina region are roughly 10.500 square kilometres of territory, if it is so simple, why couldn't NATO and the UN do it? I concede that the parallels will not be perfect but, nevertheless, we need to examine in this case what were the real security possibilities? What were the resources of the Croatian civilian government, the Croatian Ministry of the Interior the Croatian army to restore this order? Mr. -- the Prosecutor yesterday openly stated that this was a situation where, according to the statistics we cited to you at the beginning of this opening statement, 44.000 Croats lived in this area in 1991. By 1995, there were less than 500. That means 43.500 people and their families came back to an area that had been devastated. NATO and the UN in explaining why they could not keep control of Kosovo said the same thing: "We cannot keep control of the situation where people return to their homes and decide to take the law into their own hands an or to seek vengeance." The evidence will show on the basis of the correspondence that you will be given in this case that the Croatian authorities, military police, civilian police and others did not simply sit on their hands and do nothing as this situation continued. There is constant correspondence between Croatian institutions throughout this time period. Meetings are held because the intent was to ensure that the plans and orders that had been issued immediately prior to Operation Storm be implemented and be effective. The fact that the Croatian authorities were not fully effective does not mean that they had criminal intent. We ask the Trial Chamber to keep that fact in mind. We ask the Trial Chamber to note the comparisons that we will make and the questions we will ask of the international witnesses in this case and ask specifically what steps again were so obvious that the failure to take them amounts to recklessness or wilful indifference by the Croatian government. Nevertheless, documents from this time period, from both the ministry of the interior and the military police show that measures were being taken. I'm not here to say that all measures were effective or that all crime was prosecuted. Nevertheless, these are the statistics on the 16th of September, 1995, of the military police. According to General Lausic -- if -- Madam Registrar, if you would show the document. General Lausic filed a report on the 16th of September. I again remind the Trial Chamber that he was the head of the military police. The report is important for a number of reasons. First because in a military sense, the person who is in command of particular forces is the one who then files a report at the end to explain himself and what his forces had done under his command. It was General Lausic who filed a report about what the military police had accomplished in the six weeks from the beginning of Operation Storm until the 16th of September. This is a strong indication, Your Honour, that the Prosecution's theory as raised yesterday that General Gotovina was in command of the military police is simply false. In addition, this document from Mr. Lausic shows what the Croatian military police had done, and it says: "The military crime police, in collaboration with the RH MUP crime police, processed 321 crimes." Thirteen murders. Then beneath this, 18 cases of HV members dying accidentally. There are 191 cases of torching, 13 cases of setting explosives, and 86 cases of looting, theft. Of the known perpetrators of the above crimes, 79 members were HV members and 274 were civilians. On the 2nd of October, minister of the interior, Minister Jarnjak filed a report with the state prosecutor in Croatia, advising the state prosecutor of what had been accomplished thus far. This will be tendered into evidence for the Trial Chamber as well. On the 2nd of October, you can see a breakdown from police administrations from the period of 22 August to 2 October of murders, burnings and mines, and removal of property, which is essentially theft. You can see in Zadar-Knin 28 murders were being investigated, 162 cases of arson, three of setting explosives, and 132 of theft. Sibenik, you'll see statistics for Sibenik as well and then beneath that an overview of the number of on-site investigations and perpetrator profile. And again in the Zadar-Knin police administration, 192 conducted on-site investigations, known perpetrators -- sorry, we translated this last night so I will just tell the Trial Chamber. Zadar-Knin, 28 HV members, 194 civilians, and 1 person wearing a military uniform but who was in fact a civilian, and 15 unknown perpetrators. These are statistics which again we will not say that this meant that all crime was processed in the area, but it shows an intent by the institutions of the Republic of Croatia to process crime and, moreover, from the perspective of our client there was no reason for him to suddenly come back to Croatia and impose himself in some form of what can only be described as a coup d'etat to take over control from the legitimate civilian government.
